In accordance with a resolution of the Grand Lodge of this State,
ndopted May 16tl1, A. L. 5857, the extra copies of the Proccedof the years 5855 and 5856, which had been reserved by
the Grand Secretary for that purpose, have now been bound in the
an.me manner as the volume containing the transactions from the organization of the Grand Lodge to and including the Communication of
May, A. L. 5854, heretofore re-published by the Grand Secretary, under its authority. This system will doubtless be continued in the future, and thus the proceedings of the year 5857 will appear with those
of the succeeding year, after the next Annual Communication, as Vol-

ume III. of the series.
It will be observed that, in this volume, the index for each year's
transactions immediately follows them. This happens in consequence •
of the continuance of the page numbers through the index of the
first year, an error which will not occur hereafter.

never appealed to in vain ; for his liberality was as proverbial as his
name was extensively and favorably known. I have felt it due to the
memory of one who has proved himself so eminently kind and charitable,
to reeord this slight testimonial in his favor.
We have lost also the ,tirstJ'unior Grand Warden of this Grand Lodge,
Bro. SASCIIEL Woons, who was first Master of' Welltern Star Lodge,
No. 2, one of the three that formed this Grand Lodge. Others, too,
of our brethren, have embarked upon the bosom of the Jordan of Death,
and ·have bidden us a last farewell. " The eternal country for which
they embarked, returns us no intelligence of their safe arrival," but we
rest in the hope that they have been "safely moored in a peaceful
harbor," and that the veil of Death has been removed, and the light of
Immortality has burst upon their unclouded vision in the Holy SpiritL. and whither they have gone. We should feel grateful indeed that
so very few of our ,brethren have been summoned away from our midst;
for in p
· n to our numbers, there have been perhaps a fewer
numbe
aths among us during our separate Masonic existence, than
in any other Masonic jurisdiction in the world for the same period.
The pestilence has paid u.s but one short visit, and finding no abidingplace in our bright and sunny atmosphere, it bade us a speedy adieu.
Would that our brethren elsewhere had been so fortunate as we ; for
we have had many and sad accounts of their bereavements and sorrows.
}]specially has this been the case in the Southern States. For a season,
no locality or walk in life seemed to be exempt from the ravages of
disease and death; and in addition to the ever-to-be lamented Grand
:\laster HILL, of Louisiana, Past Grand Master JoIIN GEDGE was
summoned suddenly into the presence of the Most High. Seldom had
we received intelligence which fell so heavily on the heart as this. We
knew how to appreciate his virtues and talents, for we had known him
long and intimately. The prominent part which he bore in the difficulties
at one time unhappily existing in Louisiana, and which he was mainly
instrumental in bringing to a happy termination, elicited an exhibition of
talent, and developed resources, which were never after found wanting,
and which made him a guiding and guardian spirit of Masonry in
Louisiana. · In him the ]fraternity has lost one of its brightest ornaments, and the . brethren of Louisiana one of the most. talented and
distinguished of their number.
Other jurisdictions, too, have suffered their losses. Massachusetts
has lost one of her aged and venerable representatives of the past, Past
Grand MMtcr CALEB BUTLER. Virginia, her presiding Grand Master,
EDMUND PENDLETON HUNTER, of whom it was appropriately reml'irked
that "none knew him but to love him, and those wl10 knew him best,
loved him 'most." Michigan has lost Past Grand Master .JEREMIAH
Mo@s. · Illinois, P,aat Deputy Grand Master CARDL'm ,JACKSON; and
the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of England, a Past Junior Grund
Deacon, PETER THOMPSON, who well deserves a favorable notice. He
was J~ife-Suj)erintendent of every Masonic Charitable Institution in
England, and for thirty-four consecutive years was seldom· ever known
to mis!! a meeting of 'his Lod~e, unless prevented by sickneRs. Truly

Among the first, and perhaps the most important of my official J?-Ots
wnK the assembling of the Committee on uniformity of work, appoil).t!'l~

by my predecessor, under a re~olution of the Grand Lodge, at its l~
Annual Communication. A majority of them having assembled .aj.
Aacramento on the 4th of J'uly last, pursuant to previous notice, the
Masonic Hall in that City was kindly furnished for their accommodation,
and they organized and proceeded t-0 business. · After much discussion,
nnd a free interchange of opinion, it was agreed to aq:>pt the wor~ as
<;xemplified by our worthy Past Grand Lecturer, the Right W orsh1pful
Brother ISAAC DAVIS, with such alterations and emendations as should
be approved by a majority of the members present. And in due course
of t1me, at the end of a somewhat laborious session, .the desired object
was accomplished, ai1d a system agreed upon, which is probably as free
f'rom error as any which could lrnve been devised under all the circumstances. The mode of work adopted will doubtless be presented in due
time for your consideration, and allow me to express the hope that its
relative merits will be discussed in a becoming spirit of kindness an.d
consideration, and that its imperfections, whatever they may be, will be
quietly remedied, without rashly condemning the whole on account of
real 01· s11pposed defects in some of its parts.
The Committee having selected the Ritual exhibited by Bro. DAVIS,
ns a. basis for the system which lias been adopted, I appointed him as
the best qualified and most appropriate person to teach it, and . issued a
Circular (No. 2,) appropriate to the occasion, a copy of which is herewith transmitted. It affords me pleasure to be able to state to the
Grand ]~odge, that in ·accordance with the recommendations contained
therein, a goodly number of worthy and intelligent brethren have
prnmptly cmue forward, and qualified themselves to dispense light and
instruction to their respective J. . odges and neighborhoods, after the
manner of its requirements. And when we add to this number the
members of the Committee themselves, who are presumed to have been
zealous in their advocacy of a system which they had themselves revised
and adopted, may I not congratulate this Grand Lodge, and the
1!'raternity at large, on its supposed wide dissemination, and the cheering
prospect ahead of the final consummation of our wishes in that behalf.
It is neither necessary nor proper to give my individual approval of the
work of the Committee as a reason for my having made every legitimate
effort for its dissemination among the Lodges. My simple duty as an
individual Mason, and my weightier ones as the Representative of the
Craft, during the interim of the Grand Lodge, made it incumb~nt on
me to use every proper and possible exertion on all occasions, to comply
with its known will, as expressed by itself, or through its lawfully
authorized Committees; and this I have endeavored to .do without
regard t-0 any special preferences of my'own.
•

among the Lodges, more general, and probably, more correct. The

When we take into c.onsidera,tion the fact that 0ur (lra11d Lodge has
hccn in existence only five yea.rs, and t.'hat. it was formed oft.he smallest

[425]

14

15

admissible number, there being only three Chartered Lodges then in
existence in California, (they holding under the several Jurisdictions
of l>istrict of Columbia, Missouri and Connecticut,) with an aggregate
membership of but little over half a hundred, we may well be astonished at the result which now meets our view, whilst contemplatingthe
unheard of spread of Free Masonry on these distant shores. There is
no parallel to be found in its annals for so rapid an increase, nor can a
more apparently healthful or prosperous condition;probably be indicated
elsewhere, than is to be found in this possible Ophir of the ancients.
Yet appearances are often deceptive, and the elements of the storm arc
frequently engendering when the sky seems brightest and least likely
to be overshadowed with clouds. The trite saying that "in the midst
of life we are in death," is no less true. than that in the midst of prosperity we are surrounded by adverse, though unseen influences, and
while we are rejoicing at our safety, the clements of destruction may
be quietly infusing themselves into the very fountains of our existence.
We are prone to become thoughtless and careless, during a period of
fancied security, and trusting to the calm surface of the common sea
of events, to throw ourselves carelessly upon its bosom, and drift with
the tide, heedless alike of our point of destination, or of the company
we suffer to embark with us. It is thus that an unparalleled state
of prosperity, even in Masonry, may in the end be productive of'
untoward results. The watchmen sleep at their posts, the avenues to
the Temple cease to be guarded with that unrelaxing vigilance that
should ever characterizG their sentinels, and we find when it is too late,
that our sanctum has been invaded by mercenary adventurers, who with
unclean hands and impure hearts, have smuggled themselves, as it
were, into a fraternity, the principles of which have no affinity with
the sentiments by which they arc actuated, and the teachings of which
arc, and ever must be, utterly at variance with their feelings and practices. Such may be the case with ·us even now, and beneath this
verdent surface of our fair land of Masonry, may lie concealed the
volcanic elements of' discord and confusion. Whilst contemplating
then with pride and exultation our numerical strength, and happily
rejoicing at this outward indication of prosperity, let us redouble our
diligence., guard with increased vigilance the outer door, and ever bear
in mind, that our strength and safety depend not so much upon our
numbers or our wealth, as upon the general diffusion and practice of'
the sublime principles of our Order. A chosen few, with even an
empty Treasury, but rich in those priceless jewels of Masonry, the
remembrance of its precepts and its duties, are infinitely more desirable, and of greater worth than myriads of an opposite character, with
all the worldly emoluments that could be heaped upon him.

I received a commumcation from tho G. J,, of' Kentucky, bearing date
18th December last, and which, together with my reply, I deem it proper
to report to the G. L. It was in relation to tho affiliation by one of our
Lodges, (Tehama, No. 3,) of a member of' a Subordinate Lodge of
Kentucky, who was, at tho time, suspended for non-payment of dues.
Although we do not recognize in our own action, or that of' our
Subordinates, the justness of' the principle of suspending a l\:fason
from all his rights and privileges as such, simply for the non-payment
of dues, yet I conceive that we arc bound to recognize the action of
other Grand Bodies in reference to any acts of legislation aftecting
their own members, and not notoriously in conflict with the principles
and ground-work of' Free Masonry. I therefore notified the suspended
brother, and also the l\:faster of tho Lodge with which he had affiliated
of his suspension, and that it would he necessary that it be removed
under the direction of the Grand Lodge of Kentucky. It is due the
brother alluded to, to state, that his character and standing in this
country, arc irreproachable; and that his delinquency has -doubtless
been the result of' accident, or perhaps of negligence on the part of
others, inasmuch as he afforded mo satisfactory evidence of his having
long since forwarded the full amount of his indebtedness to his Lodge,
through one of its members. Tho correspondence alluded to is
herewith submitted, (C.)

The same remissness observable in memb~rs towards their Lo~ges,

rnst accumulation of labor .in his department, at an hour when his
at.t.ention is particularly needed in the arrangement of the bu.sines!'
affolrs of the Grand Lodge in a prompt and orderly manner.
Now how is this evil to be corrected ? A new enactment, to enforce
the observance of a law of similar import, which has fallen into desuetude, not from its own defoctiveness, but from the carelessness and
neglect hoth of the governed and the law-makers, is not likely to prove
of any effect while the cmises which lead to its non-observance still exist.
The Lodges must each apply the proper corrective within their own
bodies. It is the duty of the Master and Secretary t-0 see that returns
arc made out properly and correctly, and forwarded with the dues to the

DEAR Sm AND BROTHER :-I have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letier of
inquiry of Dec. 18th, 185t, relative to C. M. Cornell, a Master Mason, and member of Mt. Moriah

Lodge, Ne. 106, Louiaville, Ky., sut11pended. for non~payment of dues. I have given the mo.tter the
requisite attention, and found on inquiry that Bro. Cornell affiliated with Tehama Lodge, No. 3,
Sacramento City, some time last year, and at the time of in•titutlng the inquiry, was the Secretary
of the Lodge. I have •ubsequcntly vioited Sacramento, and hftd an interview with Mr. Cornell,
and took occasion to notify him as well as the Master of the Ledge, of his suspension. He
furnished, at my suggstion, the enclosed statement, which I believe and hope will lead to his
speedy restoration, as he seems to have acted throughout in good faith, and the excellent character
which he sustains among the brethren of SacrBiIIl.ento, e.s a man l'.Dd e. Mason, justifies me in giving
credence to his statement.
The affiliation of Dro. Cornell was in accordance with Standing Resolution, No. 24, page 60, of
the printed Proceedings ~f the last Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge. Whether or not
the doctrine set forth in that Resolution is recognized by the Grand Lodge of Kentucky, I am
unadvised, nor would it be german to the subject to enter Into a discu.e.eion as to its propriety;
my province being only to consider the facts of the case as presented from a duly authorized
source; and although our awn Grand Lodge dees not recognize in her own action, or tha.1i of her
Subordinates, the ju.tness of tho principle of suspending c. Mason from all his rights and prlvi·
leges as such, for the non-payment of due11, we feel bound to, and do recognize the action of our
sister Grand Lodges in such matters. even though adverse to our own, and regard the subject of
•uoh prohibition in the same llght in which he is presented to us through tho medium of the
jurisdiction from which he bails. All Masonic communication has therefore been Interdicted
between Mr. Cornell and Lodge• and Masons under our jurisdiction until his suspension is
removed under the authority of the Grand Lodge of Kentucky.

1b tli.e N. W. Grand Lodge of California :
'.L'he Committee to whom was referred the Address of the M. W. Grand
Master, beg leave to report that they have had the same under considerat!eo,
and have read aud examined it with great interest and pleasure. Althougl
of much greater length than such documents usually are, we find no part of
it which we could have wished omitted-no subject treated of upon which it
was unnecessary to speak; and it affords us great gralification to be enabled
to say that it sets forth no opinions at all discordant with our own, or, in our
belief, with the general views of this Grand Lodge. The Address is replete
with sound doctrine, full of wise and good counsel, exhibits much Masonic
research and information, and breathes a spirit of zeal and devotedness for
our beloved and time-honored Institution, which cannot be too highly com·
mended.
Although it will properly be the province of the several committees to
whom the various portions of this interesting address will be referred, to dis• cuss and express opinions upon the matters therein contained, we take the
liberty of emphatically pronouncing our approbation of that part of it wherein
the attention of the brethren is called to the strict and constant observance
of those moral precepts of our Order, which are1 and must ever be, the base
and foundation of its Gxcellence, usefulness nnd claim upon the good opinion
of the world. 'roo much stress cannot be laid upon tliie subject; nor can

brighteat jewe~s.

'l'hese together comprise a mass of printed matter amounting to nearly

The report will be of' greater length than has hereoofore been presented to
this Grand LoJge-greater, pe?he.pe, than will be acceptable to .it; though by
no mee.ns so ample as many of those. which OC>1111e to us from sister juriedictiorua.
This, however, should need no juatificatil:la, as the sole object which was

7

50

51

1Jought by the origination of the s7stem of correspondeuc:e now existing
among the Grand Lodges of the United States, can only be accomplished in
such a manner. It was the intention of this system to enable every Grand
Lodge, through its committees, to h1we presented to itself, and thus to be
enabled to lay before its subordinates, an abstract of all proceedings in other
jurisdictions in nny wise affecting or relating to the general interests of
Masonry; that thus, differences of opinion and discordance in practice might
be freely and widely discussed, to the great end of final unanimity and
uniformity. The time is still within our memory when the several Grand
Lodges of America knew as little of the action or opinions of each other, as
we know now of those of most of the similar Grand bodies upon tbe continent
of Europe ; and the effect was that almost as many differences in belief a.nd
dissimilarities in work existed o.s there were bodies to entertain and practice
them. The Grand Lodge of New York was among the earliest to propose to
its sisters, in the manner now generally practiced, a regular nnd constant
interchange of intelligence upon all Masonic subjects arising within their
several territories; and, though there are still many questions upon which
the various Grand Lodges of the country differ to a grl'ater or less extent,
the general result has been most beneficial and harmonious.
Believing then that it is their duty carefully to read the proceedings which
have been transmitted to us from other jurisdictions, and, briefly as may be,
to notice such portions of them as may be of common interest to the Fraternity,
or as may convey useful information to thei: brethren in this St~te, th~ Committee enter upon the performartce of their labors, commencmg with the
Grand Lodge of

Grand Lodges, would greatly tend to preserve peace and harmony in the
Order. To this opinion your Committee most cordially give their assent, and
we can with the greater earnestness call upon our brethren in otherjuriadictions to make this most just regulation a general one, as the Grand Lodge <>f
(.)a!ifornia four years ago passed a standing resolution to this effect. No
Masonic jurisdiction has probably suffered more than ours for lack of this
wise inhibition on the part of the Grand Lodges of the Atlantic Stat11s. In
11ddition to the mortification we have felt-not more out of regard for
ourselves than for the sake of Masonry at large-at seeing those who either
had, or would have been rejected as unworth;r in our own Lodges, after 11
brief visit to the East, (anciently the place of Light,) returned upon us "Free
and Accepted," through the too amiable carelessness of our elder brethrenthere is this other injustice, unintentionally perhaps, but not the less certainly
done us. 'fhe existing state of things upon this coast has made it requisite
that the rate of fees established here should be higher than it probably is in
any other jurisdiction in the United States; and many have been induced to
apply for the degrees when upon visits to their former places of abode, for the
sake of the pecuniary saving thereby accomplished. Thus the reception of
such applications, very, very numerous as they have been, has had the effect
of greatly diminishing the benevolent fund of a State, whose Masonic charities
during the past six years,-so far at least as the expenditure of money can
represent them-have perhaps more than equalled those of all the older
States put together. And it should not be the least of considerations, either,
with our brethren across the mountains, that far the greater part of all these
disbursements has been to relieve the distresses of those who, in all respects
save their Masonic ch.dins, were strangers among us, not members of our
Lodges, recently arrived, aud many of them constituting 11 portion of thnt
Vc!St horde for whom cases of "emergency" and dispe.neation had been
provided to prepare them for the California market.
·
It is a source of great gratificatioll to your Committee to observe that
many of the Grand Lodges hnve already ta.ken that which we think to be
judicious and proper action upon this subject, and we earnestly hope that, ere
long, all will concur in a regulation, which seems so eminently just, and so
likely to be conducive to the harmony and well-being of the Order upon this
Continent. We most kindly and fraternally call their attention to the
proposition that when, for years after their attainment to "lawful age," m~m
have resided in the midst of Masonry and in the neighborhood of Lodges,

The Grand Master of .Alabama again directs the attention of hiS brethren
to a subject which has long claimed much consideration at the hands of the
several Grand Lodgee-an absence of uniformity in the work. He attributes
the difficulty in that jurisdiction to three causes principally: the too rapid
muhipli<i&tion of the Lodges ; the election by them of incompetent and
inefficient officers ; and the frequent alteration of the work by the Grand
Lodge. . The first two evils, we fear, are not confined to the State of Alabama. Masonry has of late attained a degree of popularity which has
become a fruitful source of anxiety to those reflecting and thoughtful brethren
who have at heart eineerely the best interests of their Order; and who
desire to see no spot upon the purity of its principles, or doubt in regard to
the usefulness of its objects, caused by the hurriea and careless introduction
within its portals of those who may refiect discredit upon us with the world.
That Lodges 11hould have quickly multiplied, was but the necessary consequence of the rapidity with which initiations have taken place, and the
membership of the Order thus have been increased ; and this is especially
applicable to our own jurisdiction. An unwise and-if we may be permitted to say it-unmasonic spirit of rivalry seems to have existed among
some of the Lodges, as to which should fastest increase the lists of its
membership; and perhaps the consequent accumulations to the Lodge fund
have not been foi·gotten among the incentives to the race. While such a
spirit is permitted in any wise to influence their acts, it is but too evident
tht the strict scrutiny to which all who apply for the benefits and privileges
of onr institution ought to be subjected, is likely to be relaxed ; and we may
one day have cause enough bitterly to regret that seeming prosperity which
is indicated l>y numbers only. "lestina lente." Let us make haste slowly;
for, although heretofore the rapid increase of the Lodges in.this jurisdiction
has possibly ·not been more than commensurate with the sudden growth of
our population, a period of_compemtive rest has now occurred to the tide of
emigration which for six years past has sent hither its mighty flow ; and it
may perchance be wise and profitable if we too, like the weary brethren of
whom we wot, sit down to r.est and refresh ourselves. "Let us," in the
concluding words of Grand Master Clopton's interesting address, "in all
we do, keep in full view the moral position of the Order-its respectability,
11-0t so much ·i n point of numbers, as in cha.racter and talent-and endeavor,
by precept and example, to impress these truths upon the minds of the
fr&Ulmity throughout the leagth and breadth of our State.''

In consequence of the great impositions to which the fraternity there had
been subjected, this Grand Lodge now requires all traveling Ma.sons who
desire assistance in that jurisdiction, to present a certificate of good standing
from the Grand Lodge of the State whence they hail, bearing the seal
thereof, and signed by the Grand or Deputy Grand Master, and the Grand
Secretary ; and it is recommended to the brethren of Arkansas, going
abroad, that they procure like certificates from their own Grand Lodge.
A section in the by-laws of one of the Lodges-" That no greater num·
her of votes shall be required to restore an expelled or suspended Mason,
than was required for his expulsion or suspension,'' we.a disapproved and
corrected, so that a reinstatement should take place only by a unanimous
vote. This we believe to be right, although we have just noticed a case in
another jurisdiction, where a. vote of two thirds, (being the number requisite
for expulsion,) was considered by the Grand Lodge to be sufficient for that
purpose. It would seem, certainly, that an expelled Mason, so far a.s all the
rights, benefits and privileges of the Order are concerned, is as much a
stranger to it as if he na.d never been one of its members, and that therefore
his re-entrance within its gates should require the same unanimity among
those who receive him, as that which governed at his first admission.
The Grand Lodge of Arkansas has decided, in consonance with that which
appears to be the general Masonic principle, that it recognizes no clegree of
Past Master emanating from any source beyond the jurisdiction of Symbolical Masonry; and that the order of that name is o. mere honorarium, confer-

red by way of reward for present or past services as Master of a Lod~e.- not
requisite to qualify him to preside, excepting so far as it may con~ the
ceremony of installation, now in use, which ia necessary and indispenlJ1t'ble ·
"nd further, that this Order shall hereafter be conferred only by a convoca'.
tion of Past Masters who have received it, not less than three in number
who shall be affiliated with some Lodge, and shall have·a special warrant froU:.
the Grand Master for that purpose.
A tax of two dollars per annum upon each member of the Subordinate
Lodges, was levied to increase the fund for the erection ancl endowment of
S~. ~obn's College, the Lodges being charged with its collection; and a
stirring appeal has been sent forth to the brethren of that State, entreating

This fund, thus far, has reached an amount over $17,000, a portion of which

buildings.

Neither of the projects for a General Grand Lodge, or for a National Confederation of Grand Lodges, finds support in Lolll$iana. '!'be first,constituted as M11-ine originally recot'nmentled, it is not doubted would be productive
of great good to Masonry in the United States, were it possible to ensu~e u

Oommittee believe that t.b e great e!lttent of the country, and the difficnlty ·and

voDUPlll}~cation IBllted tep days, and

ment by all the Grand Lodges, which constitute both its foundation and superatructul'e, they ask-" Who could ensure that a sub'sequent Grand Lod~e,
under the apprehension of some fancied wrong, might not rescind the action
off.tA ptedecessor, thus throwing into utter confusion the jurisdiction of the
Confederacy.''
To the first proposition, we have nothing to reply, IL8 the project of a Gene·
ral Grand Lodge seems, for the present, to be entirely abandoned; and whatever our pretlilections are·, it is useless to argue in favor of that which may
not be. In answer to the second, we would only briefly observe, that any
Grand Lodge has most undoubtedly the right to undo, at one Communication,
what it has done at a previous one, in the same manner that it has the right
to do that which has theretofore been left undone, so long as its action, in
either case, relates oaly to itself, and to matters in which its constituent!! alone
are concerned. But when, by its solemn act, it has agreed with others, sovereign and independent bodies like itself, to perform, and hold itself bound by
certain covenants which it cannot violate or alter without committing an
injury upon those others, it no longer has such right. Like all governments,
as well as all individuals, it possesses the power to do wrong, but there are
certain recognized principles to restrain the one, as there are penalties to
control the other, which are both intended to prevent the exercise of such
unlawful power. Ad well' might a present administration of the political
government of a State ignore or set aside a treaty made by a preceding one
with another sovereignty, as a Grand Lodge declare itself not bound to abide
by the covenant which its predecessor had solemnly agreed upon with its
sister Masonic jurisdictions. In either case, a great wrong would be committed, and, in our discussion of this subject, we are disposed rather to argue
upon the presumption that our brethren would govern their conduct by acknowledged ~rinciples of right, than upon the supposition that they would
probably avail themselves of their power to do wrong. Your Committee be·
lieve that this Confederacy, if successfully established, may be productive of
much good, and, howsoever large the number of Grand Lodges which may
become its constituents, we would still think it very incomplete 'while a
Grand Lodge which we esteem so highly as that of Louisiana, declined to
come within its pale.

this Grand Lodge, a notification by the Grand Secretary to the Me.sonic
family throughout the world, that a sufficient number of the members of the
Lodge, ''Disciples of the Masonic Senate," No. 5, had me.de application to
the Grand Master for permission to resume their labors under that jurisdic·
tio!l ; and that in conformity with a resolution passed in 18531 he had caused
a charter to be issued to that Lodge, with its former name and number.
This, it will be recollected, was one of the three Lodges in that State which a
few years ago abjured their allegiance to the Grand Lodge, and accepted
warrants under a so-called Supreme Council of the 33d, in New Orleans,
pretending to exercise authority over the degrees of Symbolic Masonry • a)ld
. which were the subjects of certain resolutions adopted by the Grand i.odge~
of California in 1852. .A modification of those re2olutions will now be
offered in its proper place.

The remaining portion of the report proceeds to exemplify the practical
effect of the resolutions, but as that seems evident enough without more e]uc.idation, we forbear copying further. The results to which the Committee
have arrived in the foregoing, and which were sanctioned by the Grand Lodge
of Massachusetts, hiure most naturally created much dissatisfaction among
our brethren in the Grand Lodge of New York; as it will be perceived that
the resolutions are not only aimed at those persons assuming to be Masons,
who own allegiance to the "Philips Grand Lodge," the new "St. John's
Grand Lodge," the Grand Lodge of Hamburg, and AtwooP,'s " Scottish
ltite" assumption, and at others expelled, suspended or rebellious-but they
cut off Masonic interoourse with a most respect.able number of those who now
constitute a portion of the true and recognized Grand Lodge of New York;
except. upon conditions to which, under all the circu~stanoes, it is not probable that their sense of self-respect will allow them to submit. All the Masonic world rejoiced over the consummation of the celebrated '' Act of
Union," in 1850, between the Grand Lodge of New York and the ,theu 8t.
John!.s Grand Lodge; by which the latter was dissolved, a'lld it.s subordinattll'
were recehred into the Masonic family of the former; and, until this action
of !t.Iassachus.etts, '!e have hea:d no Grand Lodjfe raise its voice to question
the manner m which that umon was accomphshed. No one cloub'8 that
those who composed the St. John's Grand Lodge of that time, Were as regularly ma.de Masons as the adherents of the other Grand l'Jody; whatever wo
mal think of the lawfulness or propriety of their acknowledged Head. And,
wlule we all admit that, within lts own limite, a legitimate Grand Lodge is

The Grand Master, in conclusion, declines being a candidate for reelection,
for reasons which do him infinite credit as a Ma.eon. ''For several yea.rs,"
~nys he, ''I resisted the importunities of my brethren to allow my name to be
used for this situation, because I believed I should not be able to 'discharge
lhe duties of the office without interfering with other important avocations.
I have now tried it one year, and find that I have not the requisite leisure to
discharge the duties of Grand Master of Ma.sons of the State of New York,
u~ those duties ought to be discharged; and I cannot consent to be a Ma.sonic
tlrone, to enjoy the honors of this situation without rendering to the Grand
Lodge a proper equivalent in services therefor."

New York diarupted, and the example thus aet for future subdivisions of other

yet we cannot approve of the action of tbose Gro.nd Lodges who, so fa.r in advance of the necessity for an opinion, the propriety of which we greatly doubt,

We have yet to lea.rn tho.t there is any law of Masonry which requires that a Me.sonic jurisdiction shall o.f necessity be co-terminate with the political boundaries of a State or Kingdom ; and, adhering to
our constant theory of the entire independence and absolute supremacy of every Grand Lod~e, within its own Masonic tt>rritory, we can see no reason why
it may not, if it so please to do, peaceably divide itself into twenty different jurisdictions. New York might do even this, and each Lodge still bold sway
over as many subordinates, as now exist in some others of our Masonic sovereignties. 'fher.e is a wide difference between questions of right and of expediency. What other Grand Lodges can urge age.inst her right to do this, we
have not yet been permitted to see, except in the shape of barren assertion ;
and of the expediency of the act, she herself is the only rightful judge. We
are pleased at the decision she has made, and we hope sincerely that the question of division may be put at rest forever.

The New York Oommittee joins its voice to the universal expressions of fear
lest the late too rapid expansion of the Fraternity, and increase of its member·
ship, may result in unhappy consequences. "Though the path of the Order,"
says Bro. KING "is as yet strewn with garlands, and canopied with skies of
cernlee.n loveliness, a revulsion may come upon us--a. whirlwind may ovcttake
us, and sweep this path with desolation, and change those skies into angry
frowns of impending ruin. We feel constrained, therefore, to recommend th~
adoption ot measures to limit the multiplication of Lodges in oqr own jurisdiction, and to advise the closest scrutiny into the qualification of applicants, 11~
the most effective means to guard age.inst these dangers ; and we commend
these precautions to the Grand Lodges of the country generally."

OREGON .-Our neighbor of this Territory held her Annual Grand Communication for 1854, in the town of Salem, on the 12th of June, the R. W. ;T. C. AINswoRTH, Deputy Grand Master, presiding, and the R. W. BENJAMIN STARK,
Grand Secretary. The representatives of six chartered I.odges were present,
being all then existing in the Territory. The Deputy Grand Master, in bis
address, announces the death of the M. W. JOHN ELLIOT, late Grand Master ;
states that dispensations for three new Lodges had been issued ; (now chartered;) and mildly reproves the unfriendly and unmasonic spirit which seems,
unhappily, to have been evinced in one or more of the subordinate Lodges. He
disapproves of the practice w bicb existed in some of the Lodges of "postponing
a ballot, after it bad been taken, to some future time," in order that another
might occur when the opposing brother was not present ; and we are only surprised that condemnation of such a practice should not have been couched in
stronger terms. Its result would be that majorities would govern in the admissions to the Order, instead of that unanimit·y which is the vital principle of its
existence. He recommends the adoption of stricter regulations for the govern·
ment of the conduct of all Masons in that jurisdiction, whether affiliated or not;
urges the subject of Education upon the attention of tbe Grand Lodge; and
commends to the liberality of the Fraternity the propriety of giving aid to the
erection of tbe Washington Monument.
We remark one occurence among the proceedings which, with our limited
knowledge of the extent of Masonic powers aud prerogatives, seemed somewhat singular-the suspension of a Me.son, for refusal to obey a summons, by
the order of the Master of tl1e Lodge. And this act was approved by the Grand
Lodge, although the offending brother was restored by its order. We had
heretcifore supposed that such power of punishment resided in the Lodge alone,
and was there properly exercised only after charges were preferred and a fair
trial offered.
This Grand Lodge is in favor of a General Grand Lodge, or some equivalent
body, and authorized its Grand Master elect to represent it at the Washington
Convention. 'rbe receipts durin~ the year were $743, and the expenditures
$665; and there remained 8542, m the Treasury. The Communication con~inued four days, and the M. W. J.C. AINSWORTH was elected Grand Master,
and the R. W. BE1u. STARK re-elected Grand Secretary.

Bro. MACKEY does not approve the resolutions of this Grand Lodge in 1853,
relative to the powers of Grand Masters, and their liability to punishment for
misconduct, and goes so far as to express his disbelief "that under any circumstances can he be punished for an:y crime whatsoever, during the tinle that he
presides over the craft,'' for the reason that he could not have "that essential
Anglo-Saxon requisite, a judgment by his peers." Your Committee have no •
expectation that even the modification of this resolution which they propose
to offer, will accord with the extensive views of the prerogatives of a Grand
Master entertained by our honored brother of South Carolina ; but they do
entertain the hope that the "new regulation" which they will submit accompanying it, may remove his objection as to the impossibility of a trial by his peers.

and the W. ALBERT G. MACKEY was re-elected Grand Secretary.
TEXAS. The Grand Lodge of Texas held its Seventh Aunual Communication, in the town of Rusk, on the sixteenth day of January, 1854, the M. W.
ANDREW NEILL, Grand Master, presiding, and the R. W. A. S. RUTHVEN,
Grand Secretary. One hundred and forty-two Lodges are in existence in this
jurisdiction, seventy-nine of which were represented at this assembly. Eight
dispensations for new Lodges had be\ln issued by the Grand Master during the
preceding year. He recommends that the Grand Lodge o! Texas, signify
its disapprobation of the action of Lodges in other States, who receive arid
act upon petitions of those who are visiting or only temporarily residing
among them, e.nd mentions the provision in that State which requires a year's
residence, before 11 candidate can be eligible. He is in favor of the proposed
Confederation, and thinks it will accomplish all that was desired from a Genloral Grand Lodge, without being liable to the many objections to such an organization. He desires to see the so-called Past Master'.s degree abandoned
by the Chapters, and given only as a distinction in the Sym'Bolic Lodges, where
it properly belongs; and gives his opinion against a practice which appears
to prevail in 'fexas, the re-consideration of a ballot by the Lodges.
'l'he report of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence is by Bro. F. B.
SEXTON, and is a very able commentary upon the proceedings of the other
Grand Lodges, embracing some seventy-five pages. Bro. SEXTON is not satisfied with the manner in which the difficulties of 1852-3, in this jurisdiction,
were disposed of at the Annual Communication in the latter year. After
enumerating the charges presented on tho one hand, and counter statements
made upon the other, as they were published, and presenting the report and
resolutions of the special committee of Past Masters, appointed at that session
upon the Grand Officers' addresses, he says: "We mu&t be allowed to dissent
from this wholesale smothering of a transaction, wherein one or both of the
parties bad openly and palpably transgressed some of the most elementary and
vital principles of Masonry. * * *
If the opinion is allowed to prevail that one brother may openly denounce another as corrupt, (no matter if

*

it be the Grand Master or the humblest brother,) publish this denunciation to
the world, and when both are called. to account for it by the proper tribunal,
they can make a personal compromise of the whole matter, without suffering
auy penalty, even the slightest, as a satisfaction for the blemished reputatiol,\
or the Order-it will but invite unmasonic conduct." He is decidedly of· the
opinion that somebody-one or both the parties in this case-ought to have
been rebuked, somehow, and this is \lossibly true enough, yet no good is to be
effected by tearing open wounds, which it is hoped that time and charity may
have nearly healed.

purpose of joining another Lodge. There is ancient law for this too but we
think it, like some other of the ancient customs, "more honored i~ th~ breach
than tho observance." Oompnlso1·y Masonry is almost a solecism in terms.
Let thoae who wish to leavens depart in peace, but let our reuulations be so
fro.med herearter that they shall not share the benefits of the ae~mulations re1-1ulting from the fait~falnes.~ of others. The Gr11:nd Lodge of 'J.'e:xas, hQwever,

also declared that none ~hall visit in that jurisdiction more than th;ee times

Your Committee have already endeavored to refute some of the arguments
which have been presented against the adoption of such a form of Confederation as that proposed above, and had intended, ere this report Will! concluded,
to offer some opinions, and reasons therefor, in its favor. Butfthe unexpected

in Masonry, constituted as a General Grand Lodge. With th.is belief, they
recommend it to the favQrable consideration of the Grand Lodge of CalifO?"nia,
and will offer a resolution that it be adopted.
In conclusion, your Committee beg leave to say that, in the expression of any
opinions which may have been elicited during their examination of the various
subjects for Ma.sonic discuBSion, appearing in the several publications before
them, they have sought to broach no new theories-to teach no new doctrines
-but, humbly aware of their own limited Masonic experience and information,
(the writer speaks for himself alone,) they have endeavored to be guided in
most cases, by the judgment of those whose distinguished position in the Order
or deserved reputation for high Masonic attainments, might well entitle them
to be coosidered as authorities ; and when these have confiicted with others
equally entitled to respect, your Committee have chosen between them with
such discretion as their own poor abilities enebled them w exercise. With

In his private character he was intimately known to us, and had our entire
love and confidence. For many months we had occupied the same rooms
and broken cf the same bread with him. During his illness we had watched
orer the heavy breathings of his midnight hours, ani when bis lips had
becoll).e pallid and his eyes sunken, the faltering words were breathed into
our ear, "All is well." It was a message of joy to more hearts than one.
We felt it ere the wing of the Angel of Death brushed past us, and witnessed
the sign of distress at the moment the spirit departed for the Eteru al Country.
Let us hope and believe that the well known signal was recognized in the
Hpirit land, and the pass-word given and received, by which alone admission
can be gained into the presence of our Supceme Gi'and Master in Heaven.

After prayer by the Grand Chaplain, the object of this special communication was stated by the Grand Master, who addressed the Grand Lodge as follows : Brcth1·en nf the Gmnd Lodge of Oalijo1·nia:

The object. of our present convention is too well aud painfully known to
render any explanation necessary. The, melancholy co.use lies before us and
in our midst. Another weary spirit has gone upon its long and last journey,
and we are again reminded of the oft-taught, but too little heeded lesson
which has so many times pleaded in expressive silence with the human heart,
from the portals of the tomb. We have assembled to pay the last sad tributC1
of duty and affection to a departed friend and brother, and whilst according
it, let us not be unmindful of the serious admonition it should brill,!! to us,
who still live and move in the spl1ere of action from which it has pleased our
Divine Fatlier that he should be removed. It is not for us to extol his virtues or to dwell upon his imperfections, whatever either may have been. Let
us rather embalm the one in onr hearts, while drawing the mantle of charity
over the other; and in after days, should memory revert to any trait of character less perfect than might be required by the standard of our own errfog
judgment, let us rest in the hope ibat, in remembrance of the virtue~ he
possessed, the Recording Angel has dropped a tear upon the fault and blotted
it out for ever.
On hfa official connection with this Grand IJOdge it is 1ieerlless to comment.
It is too well kuown and faithfully remembered ·to render lanrlation necessary.
'l'he first Master of the oldest Lodge in the State, his ability and Masonic skill
soon caused him to be extensively and favorably known to the Fraternity,
and one year after the formation of this Grand Lodge he was chosen its Secretary, an office he has filled with an ability best praised by reference to his
repeated reelection, and the large vote by which it has always been effected.

Bro. ~\ A. rrhomas moved that a Committee of five be appointed to prepare and report suitable resolutions expressive of
the grief of this Grand Lodge at the untimely death of its late
Grand Secretary, and of its respect for his memoryWhich was adopted, and the Grand Master named as such
Committee, Dros. '.I.'. A. Thomas, A. G. Abell, A. llollub, C. R.
Saunders, and L. C. Owen.

the Hall by California Lo.dge, No. l, of which he was a member,
the solemn funeral ceremonies of the Order, appropriate to the
occasion, were performed by the l\I. W. Grand Master, assisted
by the assembled brethren.
The Grand IJodge was then called off for the purpose of
attending the remains of our deceased Brother to the city of
Ran Jose, the place appointed for their interment, - to be eallerl
on again at the order of the Grnncl Master.

A Notification-Is the notice by which the time, place and hour, (and frequently tlie business,) of the Lodge are communicated to the members. This
notice, every brother receiving it is expected to obey, unless his doing so
would materially interfere with his buaineas engagements. The obligation
which it imposes is a general one, and the highest penalty incurred by a vio·
lation of it, 1s forfeiture of membership.
A Summoii.s-Is a call of authority-a citation to appear .a nd answer t<>
the charges therein set forth. Or, it is an iinperative injunction to appear at
a. special meeting of ihe Lodge with which the brother receiving it is affilit1ted; or, to attend on the Grand Master, the District Deputy Grand Master, or
any committee, or other body1 authorized by the Grand Lodge to issue it.
The obligation to obey it is special and obligatory on every brother receiving
it. 'J'.he penalty for its iion-observance is expulsion, unless the pnrty offending be able tci urge a pressi'ng and positive necessity for his ex cuse.

ARTICLE VIII.
Poicers of tlte Grand Lodge.
SEC. 1. The Grand Lodge has original and exclusive jurisdiction over nil
subjects of Masonic legislation, and nppellate jurisdiction only from the decisions of the Subordinate Lodges ; and its enactments and decisions upon
all questions shall be the supreme Masonic law of the State. It shall also
prescribe such rules and regulations for the government of the Subordinate
Lodges as will, in its judgment, conduce to the welfare, prosperity, and hap·
piness of the Craft ; and may grant Dispensations and Charters for the establishment of new Lodges, and may revoke jj.nd annul the same, for such causes
as it may deem sufficient. It shall prescribe the manner, and shall require a
uniform mode of working; and may require from the Subordinate Lodges
such reasonable dues audjees, as will at all times discharge the engligements
of the Grand Lodge.

AS COLLECTED FROM THEIR RECORDS, AND PUBLISHED BY ORDER OF

THE GRAND LODGE OF ENGLAND,

1722.

3111 compliance wit~ the foregoing order, the following Ancient
Charges and Regulations are re-published. These were collected from the old records of the Lodges, and presented to the
Grand Lodge of England on the 27th day of December, 1721,
by Dr. Desaguliers, and James Anderson, D. D., who had been
appointed for that purpose, ancl after examination and revision
by a Committee of fourteen learned brethren, were ordered to be
published by that Ancient Grand Lodge, un the 25th day of
March, 1722.
W. H. HOW ARD,
Grand Master.

I. Concerning God and Religion.
A Mason is obliged by his tenure, to obey the moral law; and if he rightly
understands the art, he will .never lie a. stupid a.theist, nor an irreligious libertine. But thou¥h in ancient times Masons were charged in every country to
be of the religion of that country or nation, whatever it was, yet it is now
thougpt more expedient only to oblige them to that religion in which all men
agree, leaving their particular opinions to themselves ; thal is, to be good
men aud true, or men of honor and honesty, by whatever denominations or
persuasion~ they may be distinguished; whereby Masonry becomes the centre
of union, and the means of conciliating trµe friendship among persons that
must else havo remained at a. perpetual distance.
,

II. Of the Civil Magistrate, Supreme and Subordinate.
A Ma.sou is to be a peaceable subject to the civil powers, wherever he
resides or works, and 1s never to be concerned in plots and conspiracies,
a!!'ainst the peace and welfare of the nation, nor to behave himself unduti·
f~ily to inferior magistrates; for ns Masonry hath been always injured by
war, bloodshed and confusion, so ancient kings and princes have been much
disposed to encourage the craftsmen, because of their peaceableness and loyalty, whereby they practically answered the cavils of their adversaries and pro·
moted the honor of the Fraternity, which ever flourished in times of peace. So
that if a brother should be a rebel against the State, he is not to be countenanced in his rebellion, however be may h11 pitied as an unhappy man; and,
if convicted <>f no other crime, though the loyal brotherhood must and ought
to disown his rebellion, and givo no umbrage or ground of political jealousy
to the government for the time being, they cannot expel him from the Lodge,
and his relation to it remains indefeasible.

160
In. Of LodgeE.
A Lodge is a place where Masons assemble and work: Hence, that assembly, or duly organized society of Masons is called 11 Lodge, and every brother
ought to belong to one, and be subject to its by-laws and general regulations.
It is either particular or general, and will be best understood by attending it,
and by the regulations of the General or Grand Lodge hereunto annexed. In
ancient times, no Master or Fellow could be absent from it, especially when
warned to appear at it, without incurrincr a severe censure, until it appeared
to the Master and Wardens, that pure n~cessity hindered him.
'l'he persons admitted members of a Lodge must be good and true m~n,
free-born, and of mature and discreet age, no bondmen, 110 women, no immoral or.scandalous men, but of good report.

IV. Of Masters, Wardens, Fellows, and Apprentices.
. All preferment among Masons is grouuded upon real worth and personal
merit only ; that so the lords may be well served, the brethren not put ~o
shame, nor the Royal Craft despised : Therefore, no Master or 'W_ arden is
chosen by seniority, but for his merit. It is impossible to describe these
things in writing, and every brother must 11ttend in his place, and learn them
in a way peculiar to this fraternity: Only candidates may know, that no Master should take an Apprentice, unless he has sufficient employment for him,
and unless he be a perfect youth, havinir 110 maim or defect in bis body, that
may render him incapable of learning the art, of servinir his Master's lord,
and of being made a brother, and then a :Fellow Craft in due time, even after
he has served such 11 term of years as the custom of the country directs; and
that he should be descended of honest parents; that so, when otherwise qualified, he may arrive to the honor of being the Warden, and then the Master of
the Lodge, the Grand Warden, and at length the Grand Master of all the
Lodges, according to his merit.
No brother can be a Warden until he has passed the part of 11 Felio~
Craft ; or a Master until he has acted as 11 'Varden, nor Grand Warden until
he has been Master of a Lodge, nor Grand Master unless he has been a Fellow Craft before his election, who is also to be nobly born, or a gentleman of
the best fashion, or some eminent scholar, or some curious architect, or other
artist, descend!id of honest parents, and who is of singular great merit in. the.
opinion of the Lodg-es. And for the better and easier and more ho~orable
discharge of his office, the Grand Master has a power to choose his own
Deputy Grand Malilter, who must be then, or must have been formerly, the
:\laster of a particular Lodge, and has the privilege of acting whatever the
Grand Master, his principal, should act, unless the said principal be present,
or interpose his authority by a letter.
These rulers and governors, supreme and subordinate, of the Ancient
Lodge, are to be obeyed in their respective stations by all the brethren, according to the old charges and regulations, with all humility1 reverence, love
and alacrity.

V. Of the management of the Craft in Working.
, All Masons shall work honestly on working days. that they may live creditably on holy days; and the time appointed by the law of the land or confirmed
by custom, shall be observed.
·
The most expert of the ]'cllow Craftsmen shall be ~ppointed the Master, or

161
Overseer of the lord's work, who is' to be called Master by those thnt work
under him. The Crafti;men are to avoid all ill language, and to call each
othe1• by no disobliging name, but brother or fellow ; and to behave themHolves courteously within and without the Lodge.
1'he Master, knowing himself to be able of cunning, shall undertake the
lord's work as reasonably as possible, and truly di~pend his goods as if they
were his own; nor to give more wages to any brother or apprentice than be'.
1•eally may deserve.
'
Both the Master 11.nd the Masons, receiving their wages justly, shall be fllithi'ul to the lord, and honestly finish their work, whether task or journey; nor
put the work to task, that hath been accustomed to journey.
None shall discover envy at the prosperity of a brother, nor supplant him
or put him out of his work, if he be capable to finish the sai:he; for no man
c&n finish another's work so much to the lord's profit, unless he be thoroughly
acquainted with the designs and drafts of him that beooan it.
'Vhen 11 Fellow Craftsman is chosen 'Varden of the"work under the Master,
he Hhall be true both to Master and Fellows, shall carefully oversee the work
in the Master's absen1:e to the lord's profit, and his brethren shall obey him.
All Masons employed shall meekly receive their wages, without murmuring
or mutiny, and not desert the master till the work is finished.
A younger brother shall be instructed in working, to prevent spoiling the
materials for want of judgment, and for increasing and continuing of brotherly love.
.
All the tools used in working shall be approved by ·the Grand Lodge.
No laborer shall be employed in the proper work of Masonry; nor shall
Preemaaons work with those that are not free, with-0ut an urgent neceSBity ;
nor shall they teach laborers and unaccepted Masons, as they should teach a
brother or follow.

SEO'l'ION I.
Whenever n member of a Lodge, or a Brother, under this j11risdiction, shall
be nccused of any offence which, if proved, would subject him to suspensjon
or exp11lsion, the proceedfogs in the premises shall be conducted agreeably
to tlie following rules : Rur.E 1. The accusation slmll be made in writing, under the signature of
a Master Mason, and given in charge of the Secretary of the Lodge, who,
under the direction of the Master, shall serYe, or cause the accused to be
Merved, with nn attested copy of the charges, ten days at least, previous to the
time appointed for the examination : Provided, The residence of the l\Ccused
shall be known, and shall be withit1 the distance of fifty miles of the pl11ce
where the Lcidge, having the matter in hand, is located. If t.he residence of
the accused be at a greater distance than fifty miles, but within the State,
then, and in that case, a summons to o.ppear and show cause, forwar<lcd to him
by mail, or other conveyance, twenty da.vs nt least, before the time of trial,
shall be considered snflicient service. If his residence be out of the State,
and unknown, the Louge may proceed to examine the charges, e;i; parte; but
if kuown, o. summons shall be sent him by mail, or otherwise, four months, at
least, before the time ~ppointed for the examination.
Ru LE 2. The examination of the charges shall be had in o. Lodge specially notified and convened for the purpo~e, at which no visitors shall be ad·
mitted, excep,t as counsel or witnesscg.
Rur,E 3. The accused may select any brother for his counsel, and the witnesses shall testify,,if Masons, on their honor, as such. Hearsay evidence
shall he excluded.
RULE 4. The q11estion, ''Is the accused guilty or not guilty?" shall be dis·
tinctly put to each member of the Lodge, by name, commencing with the
youngest. 'l'he answer shall he given standing, o.nd in a distinct and audible
manner. The Secretary shall record the answer as given.
RULE 5, If the verdict be susrension or expulsion, the name of the per·
son so suspended or expelled shal be sent up at the ensuing meeti11~ of this
Grand (.odge for examination; and if no appeal be taken, the action shall
be final.
RULE (), A sentence.of expulsion shall not take effect until confirmw! by
this Grand Lodge; but shall operate ns a suspension of the delinquent, in the
me•ptime. In all cases n majority of two-thirds shall be necessary to suspei1d or expel.
SECTION II.
A suspension or expulsion of a Brother from a Royal Arch Chapter, or an
Encampment of Knights Templnrs, shall not operate as an expulsion from
the Lodge of which he is a member.

and ii is but proper to remark, that such of them as should have reported last

Since the close of our laBt Communication I have iBSUed Dispensations to open
and hold twenty-three Lodges, a list of which is herewith submmitted.
These, in addition to the Chartered Lodges, and the three whose Dispensations
were continued under the direction of the Grand Lodge, make the present
number of working Lodges one hundred, with an aggregate membership of
about four thousand. This exhibition shows the usual rapid increaRe that bas
heretofore characterized our jurisdiction, though not calculated, in my opinion,
to give rise to just grounds of apprehension, further than may naturally
attach to a rapid growth ; for I have reason to believe that the doors of our
Lodges have been guarded with increased vigilance, and that Dispensations for
new Lodges have been applied for only under circumstances that suggested the
manifest propriety of granting them.
In view, however, of the importance of a matter that has been so frequently
adverted to, and has awakened the apprehensions of the reflecting and experienced Mason, both here and elsewhere, as to the probable result, it may not be
deemed inappropriate to allude again to the danger that naturally attaches to
such an accession to our ranks, and the remissness that is too apt to obtain where
a Lodge is crowded with applications for the mysteries of Masonry. I would
through this channel also admonish the Brethren of the jurisdiction to look well
to the material they are working into the Masonic edifice. If there be any
defect, such as will not stand the test of the most rigid scrutiny, reject it,- it iR
unfit for use. It is better in a mntter of such grave importance to reject,
through the operation of a safe, even though stringent course of policy, several
worthy applicanta, than by its converse to admit one of doubtful reputation,
whatever ma;r be the motive for so doing. The former class may renew
their applicat10ns in due course of time.; and with the more intimate knowledge
of their true character that would naturally obtain after the occurrence of such
an event, are more than likely to have justice done them ; while the latter, when
once invested ·with power, are not apt to be over scrupulous a~5 to its use, either
within or without the Lodge, for the accomplishing of any desired object, and
sometimes injure both the Lodge and the Fraternity by a general reputation for
unworthiness, without the ability to define any particular act that would seciirP
their ejection.
Nor does it suffice that nothing can be said against an applicant for our mysteries. Equal diligence should be exercised in ascertaining what can be urged
in his favor. Negative virtues will not answer. His recommendations should
be of a positive nature, and show that he could add to the reputation of the Institution instead of havingto borrow from it. Otherwise, he had better remain
without the Lodge until better qualified to prove useful within it.
Beware, also, of any temptation to do work for the sake of adding to the pecuniary resources of the Lodge, or including among its members those who
would wield influence by means of either wealth or station. Forget not to try
the rich and the poor, the man of influence and him of humble station by the
game standard, and fearlessly reject both alike, where there is any moral unfitness that would require correction in the Lodge. A Masonic Lodge is not a
proper place to admit an unworthy applicant for the purpose of correcting
errors and irregularities that existed previous to his proposed introduction.
'fhere is danger in the experiment.
In addition to the Dispensations already enumerated, I hnve issued several
for special purposes, where, in my opinion, there were good and sufficient reasons for doing so, without interfering with any .provisioas of the Constitution or
Regul11tions of the Grand Lodge. I deem it unnecessary to enumerate them on
this occasion, as their general tenor can be ju~ged of by reference to those
granted during my first term of service ; and my correspondence during the
past year will exhibit them, together with moRt of my ofllci11l acts, should any
occurrence render such exhibition desirable.
I should-not omit. however, to mention that. I have granted one DiRpensation

of peculiar importance ; more so, perhapii, than any other during my official
connection with this Grand Lod~e. I allude to one granted on the 29th day of
J<:ebruary last, to open and hold m the City of San Francisco a Lodge of instructwn, to be composed of the officers and such of the members of the Subordinate
Lodges as saw prop.e~ to .unite w!th them,. for exemplifying the work, teaching
tho lectures, and givmg mstruct10n relative to all the rites and ceremonies of
the Order that can properly be exhibited before Master Masons I allude to
Lhis Dispensation as one of more than usual interest, for severai reasons not
the least prominent of '!~ic~ is, that Lodges of th!s description will, in my ~pin­
ion! prove valuable aUXJhanes towards the establishing of uniformity of work, a
desideratum once deemed almost beyond the possibility of accomplishment
though, of late, proving itself to be of practical attainment. I have no doubt but
that the formation of this Lodge, vested as it is, with such powers only as are
necessary to the collllummation of its purposes, will lead to the establishing of
others of like character in other parts of the State, and increased facilities for
the more easy attainment of the work and lectures of the Grand Lodge will

thereby be afforded the Brethren, generally, of the jurisdiction.
_There are oth;r benefits which will n11turally follow the more frequent assemhlmg together m one body of the me~bers of the diffe.rent Lodges, united

I have vlBlted a nm~ber of the Subordinate Lodges during the past year and
have held converse with many of the Brethren1 both within and withou't the
~odge. I have met v.:ith no vio~ations of Masonic Law or departure from established usage, of sufficient magnitude to demand a special notice through this

I will commence with such amendment.R to the Constitution as have already
beeu proposed, and follow with suggestions relative to one or two others, that
I think might be proposed and made with both propriety and advantage.
It has been proposed to amend Sec. 5 of Art. X. so as to reduce the minimum
price for confernng the degrees to either fifty or forty dollars. The contemplated reduction could in rny opinion be made with manifest propriety, in the
present financial contlitiou of the country, which is by no means so favorable as
when this feature of tl1c Constitution was originally introduced. To country
Lodges, particularly, woultl the proposctl r eduction prove both acceptable and
adl"antageous. Tbl"re are many ,good antl worthy men, antl of a class that furnishes the best of material for usefulnc88, who would become applicants for the
degrees were their means of payment more ample, or the minimum cost reduced,
so as to admit of Lodges conferring them for a smaller sum. Experience has
shown, also, that a high rat.e of chnrges has not prevented the introduction into
the fraternity of unworthy men, who, when promptecl hy me1·cenary motives, are
not apt to withhold their appllclltious on account of the cost. The proposed
amendment seems to me to be unexceptlon11ble in it~ geueral application, from
its not preventinl\' Lodges ti-om either eAtablishing or continuing n higher rate
of charges, at their option.

My opinion is also adverse to the proposed amendment to Sec. a, of Art. III.
of the Constitution, which would require that "No Communication of this
Grand Lodge shall be continued for a longer period than six days." I do not
think that its adoption would prove of any practical benefit, and am apprehensive that it would have a contrary tendency. We have no assurance that the
business of the Grand Lodge can be properly disposed of within any reasonable given period, such as would render it advisable to define the precise time
of the duration of each Communication, and I therefore think that we would
act unwisely in attempting to force such a result, in the manner proposed ; and
more especially within a period, the shortness of which might hurry its action,
and induce hasty legislation-an evH of which we have already had reason to

I would suggest the propriety of changing a feature of the Grand Lodge
"Regulations relative to trials," 80 as to substitute a secret ballot in the place
of the viva voce vote, which is at present required to be given. I concur in
opinion with a tlistinguished brother who has noticed this feature of the Regu·

tendency." The reasons aasigned are such as would apply in cases of applicants for initiation, the feature becoming only the more objectionable on account of the relatfonship existing between the parties.
My attention lias, in like manner, been directed to the' expression, " Previous
Question," as" ne,\· in the Masonic nomenclature," and smacking or the leaven
of legislative infusion. I do not notice this expression for the purpose of either
approving or condemning it, as certain rules of order and propriety are necessary to the government of all deliberative assemblies, and the body to be governed is the proper judge as to what they should be. Where they either do not
exist, or are deficient in their provisions, such absence or deficiency should, of
course, be supplied.
To guard, however, against " innovations iu the body of Masonry " that
might grow out of a proneness to departure from established usage and the
iutroduction of new features, borrowed from organ~ations of a wholly clifferent
character and tendency, I would suggest that wherever there is a departure
froI?- .the old beaten track, the necessity a~d propriet.;r should be m~nifest and
positive, and not the result of extraneous mfluences ot that progressive character that attach more 11ppropriately to political organizations. Justice aud
right, the paramount governing principles of a Masonic assemblage, are not, by
being circumscribed within the boundary of restrictive regulations, to be made
to swerve from their appropriate application for the sake of conforming to parliamentary usage or technical requirements. Their uue enforcement may sometimes even require a departnre from such usage ; anu when of otherwise manifest propriety, and not contrary to an express regulation, such departure should
be had,
The Rubject of jJorder jurisdictiou should, in my opinion, engage the attention
of the Grand Lodge during the present Communication. Some regulations
~honld be established to prevent any difficulty that might by possibility occq1·,
and <lo away with the inconvenience of a too strict application of geographical

prove a better governing rule than mere geographical lines. A strict adherence to the latter might prove a matter of serious inconvenience to applicants,
and not promotive of the interests of the Lodge.

The subject of uniformity of work will, I presume, engage the attention of

the work, and the rehearsal of the lectures of each degree, so as to enable the

necessary and proper. I see no obstacle in the way of a proper disposition of
the matter, under a candid and dispassionate i~vesti~ation, such as is. justly. Its
1lue. Masonry has nothing to fear from such mvest1gation. There 1s nothmg
within its body that can not with propriety be subjected to the test of reason and
common sense, and where anything is found incapable of abiding such test, it
Mhould be rejected as unworthy our consideration. These remarks I ?On~eive to
be particularly applicable to its Ritual, where it is amenable to the obJect1on of a
redundancy of verbiage, or inappropriateness of diction. It should, I think.
be composecl of the fewest number of words, fraught with the most appropr!ate

~tructure and requirements of the language.

You will pardon me for agam alludmg to the weighty respons1bihty resting
upon you, no less than myself, as representatives of a wide-extended and rapidly
increasing brotherhood, whose interests are necessarily involved in our action,
nnd their prosperity and .well-being dependent upon the faithful and efficient
discharge of the trust which they have committed to our care.
This can be done only by the exercise of extreme caution an~ circumspection
in all our acts, whether of a local or general character, and with an eye to the
general good, no less than the local benefit to be conferred.
Jn the pursuit of any favorite object, and with the imperfection~ naturally
attaching to us, our feelings are ever prone to enlistment, and are lia~le .to receive a prejudicial tinl!'.e. if car£> be not taken to circnmtoCribe them w1thm the

due bounds of Masonic propriety. When of 11 local origin and character, and
tinctured with an illiberal and sectional prejudice, they become unworthy alike,
both of the Lodge and the individual member who may entertain them, and should
be discarded as inimical to our best interests, wherever or however they may be
exercised. There should be no benefit sought for or conferred, that would in the
slightest degree involve the sacrifice of a correct principle, or infringe upon n
j11st right. Our 11ighest and most legitimate heneflts are of 11 social and moral
char11.cter, and are founded in interests that arc not liable to clRllh when their
pursuit is divested of all impropriety of motive. Corresponding action is likely to follow what may be regarded as the originating and governing motive
that led to it. While then our motives are pure aml correct, we ma7 with confidence expect to realize the acknowledged purposes of our organization, and
confer benefits of a character that will meet with a just appreciation on the part
of a numerous and enlightened constituency. It is thus, too, that we may expect to gain the approval ancl secure the aid of Hn.r, whom to invoke as our
Supreme Head is but a solemn mocke1·y, unless the sincerity of our motives can
he evinced by the correctness of our action. May such be our course, and may
HE, whose aid we have invoked, and who, as l\U auxiliary towards the accomplishment of His all-wise purposes, has brou~ht us safely through the trials of
the past, and spread before us tlw anticipations of a bright and useful future,
watch over our deliberations, purify our hearts with the controlling influences
of those immutable principles by which we profess to be governed, and prompt
us continually to the exercise of every feeling of heart and faculty of mind, that
will promote the true interests of the Craft, and make onr deliberations a hle~~­
ing to the Lodges and Masons of our jurisdiction. ·

Very fow have been preserved, Md it certainly is desirable that we should not

our existence, have now an opportunity to .profit by their experience. The

accumulated; -the only additional expense then incurred being that for bind·

at the present Communication, viz. :
To amend Section 1, of Article VII., by inserting after the words, " from the
State," in the second line thereof, the words-" or inability from any cause."
To amend Section 5, of Article X., by striking out the words" seventy-five,"
in the second line thereof, and Inserting in their stead the wordHfifty."
To amend
the same section in the same manner, substituting for "fifty," the
word
"forty."
To amend Section 1, of Article XIII., by a proviso that any proposed amendment or alteration of the Constitut.ion sliall be presented before the election of
Grand Officers; and, at the succeeding Communic1ttion, shall be voted on prior
to such election.
To amend Article X., by adding a 11ew section thereto, as follows :
" SEc. -. No brother shall be eligible to the office of Master of a Chartered
Louge, unless he shall have served as Warden of some Lodge."
To amend Article III., by striking out the first section thereof, and inserting in
its stead the following :
"SEc. 1. The Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge of the State of
California, shall be held in the City of San Francisco, on the second Tuesday in
May of each year."
•
To amend the same Article in a similar manner, substituting for "Snn Francieco," "Srreramento."
To amend Section 1, of Article III., by striking out the word " first," hefort:
"Tuesday," and inserting instead thereot; the word "3econd."
To amend Article III., by adding thereto the following section :
"SEc. 3. No Communication of this Grand Lodge shall he continued for I\
longer period than six days."
