fourth day of December, the M.·. W.·. DAVID CLOPTON, Grand Master, presiding,
and the R.·. W.·. ARMAND P. PFISTER, Grand Secretary. Of the two hundred and
eight Lodges then existing under this jurisdiction, one hundred and seventy-five
were represented, the number of Lodges having been increased by twenty since
our last Report.
The address of the Grand Master, like that of the preceding year, is an able
and instructive paper, the earlier portion of it being a recommendation of such
careful, just and harmonious action as should characterize the proceedings of a
body representing the Masonic intelligence of a great State. " Other assemblies," writes he, " may indulge in partial legislation, and yield themselves to
be controlled by motives of selfishness. The partisan legislator may stop to
inquire how this or that measure may affect the dominancy of his party ; and,
even when questions of state or national importance arise, may draw a screen
between his vision and every other portion of the country, and look, with steady
eye, to his particular section only. Not so in places or on occasions like the present. Every Brother, when he enters the door of this Hall, should be impressed
as if there were inscribed in legible characters above it, Equality and Jmtice;
and, whilst within, should keep in mind that we are all engaged in the same
mission, and all advancing to the same destiny." He announces the death of
the M.·. W.·. NIMROD E. BENSON, a Past Grand Master of that State, and gives a
beautiful and feeling tribute to his memory. He adverts to the proposition
presented in 1853, by Bro. FOSTER, of Missouri, for the settlement of the difficulties in the jurisdiction of New York, by their reference to the Grand Lodges of
Virginia and Massachusetts; and declares his satisfaction with the reasons offered by the Grand Lodge of New York for refusing the suggested mediation.
We are pleased to see that the opinion of a Mason so distinguished as Bro.
CLOPTON, corresponds with that which we presented in our report at the last
communication. We then quoted at some length from the report of the New
Tork Committee on that subject, and think now, as we did then, that the arguments it contained against treating in any manner with the rebellious and unlawful organizations within that jurisdiction, were good, conclusive and
unanswerable. He recommends the concurrence of that Grand Lodge in the
project for the establishment of a National Confederation of Grand Lodges, and
was himself named as a delegate from Alabama to attend the Convention held at
Washington in January, 1855, the proceedings of which were laid before this
Grand Lodge and assented to, at its last Annual Communication. A great portion of his address is given to the consideration of the proper disposition of 11
fund which had accumulated in the treasury, and which, it appears, was originally intended to be used by the Grand Lodge for educational purposes. The
disposal of this fund, now amounting to about $17,000, has for some time past
been a vexed question with our Alabama Brethren. At a preceding Communication, a Committee reported in favor of its distribution among the subordinate
Lodges, and this proposition having been adopted, another Committee_was appointed to carry out the project of the first, as soon as the views of the various
Lod.ges in the State thereupon could be ascertained. These were found, at this
Communication, to be largely in favor of the proposed division, and a third
Committee was directed to make the requisite apportionment. But we learn
from an appendix to the proceedings, that, owing to some oversight of the
Grand Lodge in rejecting a portion of the resolutions under which they were
authorized to act, this last Committee found themselves unable to proceed, and
thus the money still remained in the treasury for another year. We cannot avoid
expreesing the opinion that this is fortunate for Alabama, and we hope that
other counsels will have prevailed at the succeeding session ; for it certainly
seems to be a subject for regret that a fund so handsome, and which might be so
beneficially employed, if held together, should be frittered away and wasted, in
effect, by being scattered among more than two hundred subordinate Lodges.
Bro. CLOPTON retired from the Grand Mastership at this Communication, he
hayipg seni:ed three years, and being, by the Constitution of that Grand Lodge,
ineligible' for a further period.

ARKANSAS.
The Grand Lodge of this State, like that of Alabama, holds its Communications at so late a period thai we seldom, if ever, obtain its proceedings during
our current year. The latest we have from Arkansas are those of the Annual
Communication commenced at the City of Little Rock, on the sixth day of November 1854 theM.·. W.·. LuKE E. BARBER, Grand Master, presiding, and theR.-.
w.-. TiioMAB D. MERRICK, Grand Secretary. There were then eighty-six Lodges
under this jurisdiction, sixty-one of which were represented ; showing an increase
of twelve Lod~es during the year preceding.
Your Committee were struck last year with the beauty of the Address presented by the Grand Master of Arkansas, and the ope we now have before us is none
the less entitled to our praises and respect. In felicity of diction and argumentative ability, it is equaled by few and excelled by none of the many papers
emanating from similar sources which have come before our eyes. A great portion of that for the present year is devoted to the discussion of a domestic matter
- the refusal of two of the subordinate Lodges to obey an edict of the Grand
Lodge imposing a specific tax upon the members within its jurisdiction. This,
as our'Iast report exhibited, was a levy of two dollars per annum on each affiliated Mason in the State ; and was voted at the preceding Communication, for
the vurpose of increasing the fund for the erection and endowment of St.
J ohnrs College - a Masonic Institution projected and already commenced by
the Grand Lodge. As your Committee understand the matter, the disobedient
Lodges refused compliance with the requisition of that body, not because they
were hostile to the purpose for which the proceeds of the taxation were to be
employed- for the projected College seems to have met with general favor but from a belief that to impose a tax, for any purpose, beyond the amount required for the necessary expenses of the Grand Lodge, was unlawful, unauthorized, and, in the language of the resolutions which they presented, " subversive
of the true and genuine principles of Free Masonry." This question is one of
no ordinary importance. Although there is little. necessity , existing in this
jurisdiction at the present day for an expreesion of the conviction forced upon

An amendment to the Constitution was adopted, providing that any Master
Mason who neglects for twelve months to become a. member of some Lodge in
that jurisdiction, shall not be permitted to visit, nor be entitled to any of the
rights and privileges of Masonry. Having written at length last yel\r upon the
subject of non-affiliation, we shall only add the expression of our gratification at
seeing, not only in Georgie., but in so many of the Grand Lodges of the United
States, a stern and increasing determination to combat this gigantic evil.
When such a law shall have become universal in the land, a great support will
have been added to our ancient edifice.
From the Report of the Trustees of the Southern Masonic Female College, we
observe that this Institution, under the care of the Grand Lodge, is apparently
prospering and increasing in usefulness. A certain number of the daughters of
Masons in indigent circumstances are to be educated free of charge, to be added
to hereafter, as the funds of the Grand Lodge shall enable it to do so. Five
only a.re now proposed ; one to be selected by tbe Grand Master from the State
at large, and one by each of his Deputies from his particular District.

A plan was presented for the establishment of that great desideratum, u.nlform1ty of work. The jurisdiction was to be apportioned into eight distrleta,
from each of which one delegate was to be elected by the Lodges compr~
therein. These delegates were to e.BBemble with three skillful brethren appointed by the Grand Lodge, one of whom to be th\ Grand Lecturer, and remain in
session until perfect uniformity and agreement In the work and lectures should
be arrived at. Each delegate was then to return to his own district and open
a Lodge of Instruction, which should be attended by the Master of each Lodge
in that district, or some one by him appointed for that purpose. The Grand
Lodge Committee and the eight delegates to be paid a per diem and mileage
from the Grand Treasury, and thereafter no dispensation to be issued to form a
new Lodge unless the petitioners presented, in addition to the usual recommendation, a certificate from the District Instructor that one or more of them understood the work thoroughly, as taught by him. This plan was adopted, with the
cautious proviso, that If the eight delegates should adjourn without establishing
some system and perfecting themselves therein, they should receive no pay.
A service of plate costing $1,320, was presented by the Grand Lodge to Past
Grand Master WM. SHEETS, as a token of its appreciation of his arduous and
successful services as Commissioner of the Grand Lodge Hall ; and a very
interesting relation of the manner in which this enterprise had been conducted,
is given in the Address of Grand Master LAWRENCE on the occasion, and the
response of Bro. SHEETS.
The Report of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence, is a paper of some
thirty pages, by Bro. WILUAM HACKER. He seems not to have been in very
good humor with many other similar Committees, and appears to have been
greatly exercised in spirit by some naughty things some of them have said about
Indiana.. The venerable Grand Master of Vermont gets a rap on his Masonic ·
knuckles, and receives the startling information that " Indiana is located in the
Western States." The Connecticut Committee, having noticed the Indiana practice of going into Committee of the Whole, had remarked that the usage would
be rather a novel one to Connecticut Masons, and was one, if they mistook not,
altogether unknown to the ancients. Whereupon Bro. HACKER replies most un11.nswerably, in italics, that "the Grand Lodge of Connecticut is aJJ,ogether unknown
wthe ancients." The Grand Lodges of Michigan and Wisconsin have displeased
him greatly by the adoption of a Regalia which he com·teously styles "an
absurd specimen of balderdash ; " and the uniform code of By-Laws established
by the Grand Lodge of Kentucky are such that he "could not on any account
be induced to serve as Master of a .Lodge to be governed by them." What
atrocities they contain we are not informed. New York has been abusive, and
Massachusetts has enacted an "absurdity," and altogether our good brother
seems to have been in rather an uncomfortable state of mind. Rejoicin!J in the
fact that we have said nothing in disparagement of the Grand Lodge which Bro.
HACKER defends so resolutely, we take the liberty of expressing a hope that we
shall find him more composed by another year.
A Resolution was adopted forbidding " any Member of the Masonic Fraternity
to engage in the manufacture or traffic of ardent spirits as a beverage I" And
we perceive that one suspension was decreed in the fullfilment of this edict. On

INDIAN A.
The Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, for the year 1855, was held
at the City of Indianapolis, commencing on the twenty-eighth day of Maythe M.·. w. .. HENRY C. LAWRENCE, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.·.
FRANCIS KING, Grand Secretary. There are one hundred and eighty-six Lodges
in this jurisdiction, of which all but six were represented. This Grand Lodge,
by its Constitution, consists only of its present Grand Officers, its Past Grand
and Deputy Grand Masters, and the Masters of the subordinate Lodges, or their
proxies. The Grand Master's Address is a very business-like paper, devoted
altogether to the actual state of affairs within his jurisdiction, and not elongated
by prosy disquisitions on abstract questions. He pays a feeling tribute to the
· memory of Past Grand Master ELIZUR DEMING, a distinguished Mason of that
State, who had departed this life since the last Communication i and concludes
his own Address by a. beautiful quotation from the le.st one delivered from the
same chair by the deceased.
.
We remark that this Grand Lodge resolves itself into a Committee of the
Whole upon the Grand Master's Address, the Deputy in the Chair, a practice to
which some Committees on Foreign Correspondence in other States have taken
considerable exception. For our part we can see no reason why our brethren
of Indiana should not be permitted to do their legislation in their own way.
There is too frequent a disposition to find fault with the mere local practices or
regulations of other bodies, for no better reason, generally, than that they differ from those of the body to which the writers themselves belong. Taking the
printed proceedings before us as a test, the business of the Grand Lodge of. Indiana is done with an order and regularity which may challenge comparison
with that of any in the Union ; and abundant evidence is given that its preparation has been confided to an able and skillful Grand Secretary.
A circular has been issued by order of this Grand Lodge, to the Masons and
citizens generally of the United States, soliciting funds to aid in the erection of
o. monument upon the Battle Ground of Tippecanoe. This is to be seventy feet
in height, and to ·be constructed of ~hite marble from Vermont, in th~ Egyptian
style of architecture. The ground 1s now owned by the State of Indiana, hav.
ing been donated many yea.rs ago by the Hon. JoHN T?"fON, who was u soldier
in tile battle fought thereon ; and by an act of the Legislature, the Grand Lodge

The Report on Foreign Correspondence (the first since 1852) is by Bro. J. H .
WALLACE, who, "being a young man and a young member of the Order," craves
Indulgence for " the crudities of a pen hitherto untried in the great field of
Mnsonic literature." We do not perceive that the brother's modesty has stood
seriously in his way while writing, for it is not in our recollection to have seen
opinions more positively and dogmatically expressed, nor do we remember many
Masonic papers in which are to be found terms so harsh as are sometimes employed in this. Commenting upon the action ?f .Arkansas, heretofore spoken of,
in imposing a tax to raise a fund for the erectwn and endowment of St. John's
College, he declares it "an exercise of power without a precedent in the knowledge of your Committee in all our Masonic annals " ; and proceeds to demolish
the .Arkansas edict utterly by the expression of his intense astonishment that
" such men as PIKE, BARBER and their compeers, should undertake such a pitu of
nomeme I In the language of Bro. PIKE last year relative to Mississippi •'We hope our .Arkansas brethren will survive that." As to the matter of
" precedent," the Iowa Committee need not have gone farther than Louisiana
to have found one, last year and the year before ; and so far as the merits of the
question are concerned, :Bro. WALLACE's opinion would have been entitled to
more consideration had it been accompanied by an intelligent and skillfully
written argument like that of Grand Master BARBER upon the other side. Unsupport~d .assertions, especially when in themselves e~r?ne?ue, ~re not particularly convmcing ; and the broad-axe style of composition is a little apt to lead
to forgetfulness of proper courtesy.
The Iowa Committee agree with Bro. PIKE in regard to the rights and powers
of Lodges under dispensation, and commends the project introduced by him for
the formation of a " Supreme Masonic Tribunal,'' as being just such an organization" as the wants of the Fraternity, the age and the country demand." In
noticing the proceedings of Delaware for 1854, by which it appears that in the
absence of the Grand Master, the M.-. W.-. WM. T. REED, a Past Grand Master,
presided, notwithstanding the presence of the Deputy Grand Master and both
Grand Wardens, Bro. WALLACE declares that" the idea of a Grand Master pro
tem., under the circumstances, is truly an anomaly in Masonry." It ought not
to have escaped our zeidous brother's researches among the old Regulation& of
1721, that article XIV. thereof prescribes that" the last Grand Master present,
or else the last Deputy present, should always of right take place in the absence
of the present Grand Master, or hie Deputy." Thie certainly is not the general
usage among the American Grand Lodges at the present day, but it was the
. ancient law, and may well be that in force in Delaware.
It having been proposed in the Grand Lodge of Illinois to create a new test,
by requiring an applicant for initiation "distinctly to avow his belief in the
Divine authenticity of the Holy Scriptures," a resolution was offered that "such
a requirement was un-masonic and contrary to the fundamental law of Masonry·
and that no person, in making application for the mysteries of the Order, should
be iutenogated as to his religious btilief further than as to his belief in a Supreme Being." Hereupon Bro. WALLACE remarks that the resolution was
doubtless offered by some one who was infiuenced :' not so much by the love of

an ancient land-mark as by a hatred to that bluserJ. Book " - a very violent and
apparently unauthorized conclusion, inasmuch as the resolution simply embodies
that which from time immemorial has been the letter and spirit of the law. We
have yet to learn that Masonry is especially' a Christian institution, or that it Is
a religious one at all; and while we doubt not that our own faith in the Divine
authenticity of the Holy Writings, both Old and New; is quite as implicit as
that of our Christian brother of Iowa, we do not forget that there is a very
lartre number of our brethren, as good and worthy Masone as ourselves, whose
behef does not and can not extend so far. The precepts of Masonry are moral,
not religious, and a declaration of belief in God is required, not only for the
reason given t o the candidate upon his entry, but because there is little guaranty that a man will obey the moral law, who does not give credence to the existence of a Divine .Arbiter of our future state of being. "Masonry," we are
told, "unites men of every country, sect and opinion," and as our own traditions date it's origin at a period long anterior to the advent of the Messiah, the
attempt to introduce this new test is not only an evident invasion of the primal
law, but is a palpable contradiction of the very history which we teach and
profess to believe. There is no law of Masonry which should prevent the fraternity of Christians, Jews and Mahometans ; and that Brotherly Love, " by
which we are taught to regard the whole human species as one family," and
"which conciliates true friendship among those who might, (but for their
Masonic relationship,) have ever remained at a perpetual distance," is the very
foundation, life and spirit of the Institution.
· Bro. WALLACE, however, disposes of all save the Christiane in a very summary,
and not particula:rly ftattering manner. In his opinion, any applicant who
does not believe with him in doctrine, " should be forever rejected, if for no othm
reawn than &imply because he i8 a FOOL l" Doubting greatly whether that is much
of an argument for subverting the plainest and best established regulation of
our Order, we will only add that we are as little inclined to agree with the
Iowa Committee because Ohio had preceded him in this new article of Masonic
faith, as we are to believe that we have swerved from that Temperance which
our lessons teach, because the Grand Master of Illinois has chosen to declare
that "no man can malce use of intoxicating liquors Without a violation qf his Maaonic obligatiom !"

of that body by the oracular declaration that " all their lengthy articles of confederation amount to nothing!"
More space has been given to a review of this report than we have usually devoted to much better ones, as it is couched in language such as we do not often see

we do believe that a mild and fraternal reprehension of violent words, indicating
bad temper· and worse taste, and calculated to bring reproach on the Order,
will not be greatly stepping aside from our legitimate pathway. We are instructed in a friendly manner to admonish brethren of their errors, and with the
sincere hope that our brother of Iowa will not be offended with us for the lil:>erty, we beg leave to suggest that lees positiveness in assertion, less acerbliy

Among the resolutions appended to the report. was one providing that the
ballot for each degree should be taken in a Lodge of that degree, and that trials
should be had in a Lodge corresponding to the degree of the accused. This we
believe to be good and proper doctrine, commending itself to our reason and
sense of justice ; but so far as the balloting is concerned, we do not see that
much harm will be done by retaining our present practice, notwithstanding ita
abstract and theoretical injustice. 'l'he resolution was not adopted. Another
was passed, making it the duty of the Master of a Lodge to arraign any member
for un-masonic conduct, who should wilfully disclose· his own ballot, or seek t.o
ascertain that of another. This is, beyond doubt, strictly in accordance with
the intent which governed the establishment of the secret ballot ; for that which
it is forbidden to do directly, it is certainly unlawful to attempt to do indirectly. The Massachusetts resolutions were adopted, as was also one embodying
the views of Bro. WALLACE, before treated of, upon the new test to be required
of candidates; and a Committee was instructed to report a uniform code of bylaws to be recommended to the Lodges.

exalted body was not composed of his peers ; and hence the regulation, which
ho.a been adopted by this and some of the other Grand Lodges of the United
States, establishing a tribunal of Past Gran~ Masters for such a purpose. The
announcement seems to us rather mOl'e democratic than Masonic.

KENTUCKY.
'l'his Grand Lodge commenced its Annual Communication..for the yea.r 1865,
at the City of Lexington, on the twenty-seventh day of August - the M.·. W.·.
MARCUS M. TYLER, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. J. M. S. McCoRKLE1 Grand Secretary. The representatives of one hundred and ninety-one
Lodges were present. Two hundred and seventy-five are now subordinate to
this Grand Body, being thirty-one more than were reported by us last year.
Thti address of the Grand Mast~r i~ comparatively brief. He states that he
has visited and lectured many of the Lodges during the yea.r; recommends that
other of the Grand officers do the same more frequently ; and cautions the subordinates against the employment of itinerant lecturers, or of any who have not
the property authority. He announces the issuti of twenty-one dispensations ;
and urges the strictest scrutiny of their records, and the refusal of charters to
all where these are found incorrect-very properly declaring that by doing
otherwise the Grand Lodge virtually encourages irregularities, and thereby exerts an improper influence on those committed to its care. He denounces the
use of Masonic emblems in any manner except for Masonic purposes ; is averse
to the granting of dispensations to confer degrees ; and recommends some ac
tion upon the subject of non-affiliated Masons.
The Report on Forei~ Correspondence is from the pen of the same able
writer as was that of last year- Bro. ROBERT MORRIS, now Junior Grand Warden of the Grand Lodge of Kentucky. It is a well-prepared paper, giving an
abstract of the transactions of other Grand Bodies, and of their various opinions upon some of the principal subjects of discussion during the past two or
three years. We observe that his ideas of the propriety of the Massachusetts·
resolutions relative to New York, are in consonance with our own ; and we yet
believe that some of the Grand Lodges which have so hurriedly ~Id. them,
will retrace their legislation in this respect, upon more mature reflection. He
thinks the decision of the Grand Master of Arkansas, that "a brother, a~ainst
whom charges have been preferred, has no right to be present·at the meetm~ of
investigation," to be erroneous; and, if by "meeting of investigation ' is
meant his trial by the Lodge, we think so too, for we know of no gotxl reason
·why a Mason, accused before his brethren, should be deprived of the privilege,
which, as a man, he is entitled to among his fellows - that of confronting his
accusers. The Address of Grand Master HowARD is spoken of in flattering
terms ; and his actiorr, and that of the Grand Lodge of California, in reference·
to the case of Bro. C. M. CORNELL, who had been suspended by his Lodge in
Kentucky, is warmly praised. It is due to that brother to state, that the proceedings before us show him to have been reinstated by his Lodge on the second
day of October, 1854, though no advice of that fact reached here until their re-·

GEDGE, Past Grand Master, R.·. W.·. HENRY W. HUNTINGTON, Senior Grand

DouGLAss, a District Deputy Grand Master, and Past Grand Master of Tennessee, having all fallen before the dread destroyer since the last Communication.
A suitable tribute is paid by the Grand Master to their memory, and we see
that the remains of Bro. GEDGE were deposited in a tomb especially provided
by the Grand Lodge for their reception - a proper and well-deserved mark of
respect to one who, during life, had been so useful and distinguished a member
of that body.
Grand Master Perkins refers to the too common error that the work of Masonry is Masonry itself, and that regular attendance and familiarity with the ritual,
is a complete fulfilment of a Mason's duties. These, certainly, are but the
means necessary for the preservation of the Institution, as former ages have
sent it down to us. A knowledge of the sublime principles upon which it is
founded, of the moral obligations which it prescribes, and of the practical duties which it indicates, are absolutely requisite to form the really good, true,
and accomplished Mason. He recommends the publication of such of the Ancient Charges and Regulations as the Grand Lodge shall deem obligatory, and
we observe that those of ANDERSON are presented with the proceedings. There
ean be little excuse for ignorance in regard to the Old Constitutions hereafter,
as within the past two years half the Gmnd Lodges of the country have republished parts or all of them. He is in favor of a strict construction of the language of the ancient regulations in respect to the physical qualifications of candidates, and as we notice in the report of a Committee that one of the Lodges
had initiated a man who had no legs, it may be well to allow no room for the
exercise of discretion (or the lack of it) in that jurisdiction. He censures, deservedly, the too frequent practice among the brethren of exposing their own
ballot,' and endeavoring to ascertain the character of that of others ; and a subsequent resolution of the Grand Lodge declares such conduct un-masonic. He
declares that to confer the degrees upon ministers of the gosp~l, without fee,
or to remit the fees therefor afterward, is in violation of the spirit of the Constitution, and, though " entertaining the most profound respect for the sacred
office, and being always willing to manifest it on all proper occasions, most
positively objects to the recognition of any such distinctions in our Lodges.''
He announces the issue of eleven Dispensations for new Lodges, and mentions
the proceedings at the healing of the illegally-made Masons of the Lodge, "Disciples of the Masonic Senate," now known as "St. Andre, No. 5." There are
now two of this number, "Los Amigos del Orden" being the other; and two
numbered 1, - "Perfect Union" and'' Polar Star." He declares it as his opinion that the system of District Deputy Grand Masters has proved a failure in
thiii State, and we remark at an after period that the Grand Lodge has abolished it, giving the Grand Master authority to appoint special deputies wherever he might think it proper.
A considerable space is given to the subject of the accruing liabilities on account of the purchase of the property known as the Grand Lodge Masonic Hall,
and the making provision for their payment. This was bought a year or two
ago, at a cost of $55,000, to be paid in sundry annual payments ; and by a resolution of the Grand Lodge heretofore, a special tax of two dollars per annum,
for five years, was laid upon each member of the Lodges in the State, to be applied to the liquidation of this debt. The rental of the building, as reported by
the Board of Directors, amounts at present to $7,285, per annum, which it is
thought will be considerably increased hereafter, and this revenue, when the
outstanding indebtedness shall have been discharged, it is proposed to dedicate
entirely to the charity fund. Some few of the Lodges had objected to the tax,
but the measure appears to be a generally popular one, and the Grand Lodge
seems in a fair way to carry it through successfully.
The proceedings of "Louisiana Relief Lodge, No. l," arc briefly noticed by
the Grand Master, and in a more extended manner by the Grand Secretary in
bis report. This, it will be recollected, was originally an association of several of the Lodges in New Orleans, similar to that we now have existing In San

The Report of the Committee on Foreign Correspondence is, as heretofore,
from the instructive pen of the Rev. Bro. CYRIL PEARL. He quotes at some
length from various papers treating of the" difficultiea in New York," with all
which this Grand Lodge is already familiar ; and he acknowledges the receipt
of certain communications from the so-called "Philips Grand Lodge " in that
State, giving extracts from them- a sort of qualli recognition of that body, incompatible, it seems to u~, with the position which both the writer and the
Grand Lodge of which he is ao eminent a member, have announced. He gives
the proceeding~ of tue Masonic Convention held at Washington, in full, and
urges the assent of the Grand Lodge to the proposition thence sent forth, because, in his opinion, it will tend "to remove the most serious hindrance to the
formation and useful action of a General Grand Lodge,'' - Maine, like ourselves, having been in favor of' the establishment of such a National organization. Some ten or twelve pages are occupied with extracts from the decisions
of Grand Master HUBBARD, of Ohio, probably one of the best authorities on
Masonic Jurisprudence in the United States. He complains of the non-receipt
of the proceedings of many of the Grand Lod~es, and ns we can sympathise with
him in that respect, we commend his suggestion that two copies of the transactions of each Grand Lodge, mailed at different times, should be sent by their
respective Grand Secretaries to each of the Grand Bodies with which they are
in correspondence. The ten concluding pages of Bro. PEARL'S report are devoted to the discussion of the "Objects and Aims of General Education."
These are viewed in " a two-fold aspect - the training of the human
powers ; and the acquisition of knowledge ;" which are again subdivided
into numerous distinctive heads. Interesting anrl instructive as his disser.
tation certainly is, we are as much nt a loss to know what it has to do with
matters of Masonic correspondence, IL~ we were last year in regard to his disquisition upon " The foundation for the existence and permanency of the institutions of' l''reemasonry in the essential nature and neeessitie~ of mu.n. "
Nevertheless, as he informs us that "the highest approbation has been bestowed
by our sister Grnnd Lodges on those portions of our (his) reports, that deal
most earnestly with man's spiritual nature and necessities,'' we shall be obliged
to stand corrected in our idea of the purposes for which such a Committee, as
that of which be is the chairman, was intended.
This jurisdiction is divided into ten distficts, and the reports of the District
Deputy Grand Masters, show more p1'8.Ctical usefulness than we have heretofore
discovered in any State where that system prevails. Like Missouri, the Grand
Lodge of Maine has six Grand Chaplains. No finnncic.l report is given in the
proceedings. Three days sufficed for t.he transaction of its business, including
one spent in the exemplification and establishment of the work ; and the M.-.
W.-. JOHN MILLER was elected Grand Master. and the R.-. W.-. CHARLES B.
SMITH reelected Grand Secretary.
'

His long experience and exalted position in Masonry entitle his opinions to no
little consideration, and though they do not always accord with the conclusions
arrived at by the Grand Lodge of California, we take none the less pleasure in
recording them. Alluding to the passage in Grand :Master RADCLIFFE'S AddreEs
in 1854, where he remarks that the right of Lodges under dispensation to admit member~ by amliation " is an open question, and one about which there is a
diversity of opinion," Bro. GIL'\IAN says that it onght not to be deemed an
'' open question." That if the dispensation were a matter of right, upon application, then it might be supposed that the new Lodge could add to its membership by affiliation ; but that such is not the fact. That a recommendation must
IJe had from a chartered Lodge, and the Grand Master must be satisfied that it
is expedient to open a new one ; and that if the names of those whom the new
Lodge might affiliate had appeared among the petitioners, their application
might 11ot hnve been recommendecl by the old Lodge, nor assented to by the
Grand Master.
It seems to your Committee that this reasoning is not so satisfactory as might
have been looked for from the pen of Bro. GILMAN, nnd is not enough in itself
to condemn the usage which common consent, rather than any regulation upon
the subject, has established in California. Is it not enough in reply to it to say,
that the petitioners whom a chartered Lodge can recommend as being able and
worthy "to discharge the duties of Masonry in a regular and constitutional
manner," and in whose " Masonic integrity and ability" the Grand Master has
sufficient confidence to justify the issue of a Dispensation, will be as little likely
to receive unworthy brethren into membership as any other Lodge ! Certainly
a far greater, and, in inexperienced hands, much more dangerous power is given
them in the authority to " initiate, paBB and raise ; " and If they can safely be
entrusted with the power to make. Masons, "it does not appear very dangerous
that they should be allowed the privilege of admitting those already made to
membership. That Bro. RADCLIFFE was justified in considering this " an open
question,'' the different opinions exhibited by the records of the various Grand
Lodges of the country will abundantly show. We believe, however, that in a
majority of them the usage is that which Bro. GILMAN maintains; but what
good reasons there are for the restriction, we have yet to be made acquainted
with.
The Maryland Committee, in noticing the resignation of the Grand Master of
Missouri, expresses the opinion that no installed officer of a Masonic Lodge ca11
resign his office during the time for which he was elected; but that, if from any
cause he attend not to its duties, the officer next in rank shall take his place.
This is as we, too, have been taught. The ancient Regulations make no provisions for resignations, nor do they seem to have been contemplated; and as the
succession, in case of ab1rence, has been amply provided for, It does not appear
necessary that old and generally received usage should be interfered with.
The " Protest" against the ruling of the Acting Grand Master of New York,
which was permitted to be placed upon the record of the Grand Lodge of that
State at its Quarterly Communication in November, 1853, and that which was
previously presented, by certain of its members, against the election of Grand
Master WALWOl!TH, are commented upon with some severity by Bro. Gn,lUN;
not only on account of the disorganizing doctrines they contained, but because
they were permitted to.be received, and were allowed a place in the proceedings
of the Grand Lodge. Such papers he considers ns inconsistent with t he accustomed laws of t he Order, calculated to lower the dignity of Grand Lodges, and
savoring too much of "the spirit of the age" for the safety of the Institution.
We have noticed the inJ.emperate resolution of Indiana upon the subject of
temperance. In regard to this, our brother of Maryland entertnin8 views simiilar to those we have hereinbefore expressed. very properl_y remarking that if
the stntutes of the State of Indiana prohibit the traffic in spirituous liquors, then
such traffic would be un-masonic, as every Mason is bound to obey the' laws of
the land where he dwells. But if such be not the fact, then a new feature h_as
been introduced into MMonic legislation, as unwi&e as it is unauthorize_d", inns7
much a8 it presents a new teat, unknown and repugnant to the ancient lessons of

The " Regulations for Trials " established by the Grand Lodge of California,
are condemned by the Maryland Committee, for the clause which requires that
the vote as to "guilty" or "not guilty" shall be given viva voce. This is
thought to be contrary to Masonic usage, and likely to be productive of great
mischief. As to the first proposition, we are too little acquainted with the ancient usages at trials for Masonic offences to venture an opinion ; but that the
last is true we are abundantly satisfied. There are too frequently those sufficiently zealous in behalf of the friend who may be accused, and forgetful of the
duties of 8iknce and circumapection, to relate the manner in which different members voted on this question, and thus produce no little " mischief;" and we
earnestly recommend that in these trials the vote by ballot may be substituted.
That portion of the By-Laws of our Grand Lodge which permits a call for
the ":previous question," he objects to. This he considers "a new phrase in
Masonic nomenclature," and thinks the article must have been introduced by
some brother fresh from legislative halls. The practice of going into "Committee of the whole," noticed in two or three of the Grand Lodges, is also looked upon as savoring too much of the spirit of progress, and unwisely and unnecessarily copying after the mode of proceeding in modern legislative bodies.
The prevalent mania for establishing Masonic Schools and Colleges is adverted
to, and we heartily coincide with his opinion, that as in most of the States ample
means for education are provided at the public expense, provision by the Order
for Masonic Hospitals and Asylums would be far more wise and beneficial.
The report concludes with a resolution "that a Committee of' three be appointed to employ some suitable person to prepare a history of Masonry in Maryland."
This was adopted, and the Grand Master, Bro. CHARLES Gu.MAN and Bro. J. N.
Mc.TILTON were named as such Committee.
At this session the regulation was repealed which required adherence to the
ancient law in the respect that a candidate should be of "entire limbs;" and
in its stead was adopted one similar to that set forth by the General Grand
Chapter of the United States at its last convocation. This requires that no
candidate shall be initiated, passed or raised, " whose physical defects are such
as to prevent him from conforming literally to all the requirements of the sev.
eral degrees in Ancient Craft Masonry."
Old, and wise in the ways of Masonry, as is the Grand Lodge -0f Maryland, it
has just arrived at the proposition that not more than one degree shall be conferred upon the same individual at one sitting, and that examination ·shall be
had, and proficiency proven, before advancement. There are sixteen "Grand
Inspectors" elected in this jurisdiction, whose duties we suppose to be similar
to those of Grand Visitors or Lecturers. The Grand Lodge assembles twice a
year, the meeting in November being called the "Annual" one, and that in
May the "Semi-Annual" The financial reports show the receipts from all
sources for the half year to have been $2,243. There appears to be a "Grand
Lodge Fund" of $36,600, and the Trustees of the " Graud Charity Fund " exhibit investments and cash to the amount of $13,995. The Communication was
continued during three days, and the Grand Master and Grand Secretary were
both reelected.

We remark a subject of some interest, upon which the Grand Lodge and

and thus they might soon have Lodges at work in French, Italian, Scot,ch and

The application was renewed to the Grand Lodge, and the Committee to

1f worthy and well qualified, and that she but teaches and demands that universal language which is in use wherever her influence is diffused ; that they are
not aware of any regulation of any Grand Lodge in the world which requires
the applicants for a warrant to state in what language they propose to converse
or administer the rituals of the Institution ; that there are in Boston and its vicinity some twenty-two thousand Germans, among whom are many Masons
greatly attached to the Order, but who are debarred from the enjoyment of its

The reasoning is good on both sides, but that of the Committee seems to have

There is great force in the Grand Master's concluding argument, relative to
the impolicy and impropriety of doing aught as Masons which might, in any

come to fraternize with us, not only in Masonry but in citizenship. But it is of
no avail to say to those who do not understand our language, that they must
distribute themselves among Lodges, the members of which could not examine
them, prior to their admission, and the proceedings of which they could not
comprehend, even if' admitted. To such it could only remain, either that they
lie deprived of all regular Mawnic intercourse, or that they be suffered to establi~h it iu tbe language of their native land. The last alternative is beyond
tloubt the most fraternal, and the most in accordance with the spirit of our institution~. Under thiR jurisdiction we have one Lodge, La Parfaite Union, No.

If men would unite for charitable purposes-to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and protect the orphan-they conceal their doings in secresy, clothe themselves in collars and aprons, and call i(Onn

11. The popular mdignation may not only rise to a degree winch shall blind the public

Some differences of opinion have been heretofore expressed by the Committees
of Indiana and MissiBBippi, in relation to the propriety of Lodges U. D. receiving members,- the former advocating, the latter denying it. A considerable space is again given the subject by Bro. MELLEN, and he about half yields
tbe point by proposing a regulation that all those "raised" in a Lodge under
dispensation shall be considered as members of that Lodge· and suggests, as
the necessary consequence of such n resolution, that such.Lodge have power to
grant demits. What i! the reasonable objection to a Lodge, U. D., doing all
that a Lodge of Masons may? The answer probably will be that very ready
phrase, " because it is not in accordance with the nncient usages," -this being
the constant reason offered for many existing customs, by those whose organs of
veneration are perhaps more largely developed than those which indicate the
reasoning powers. We would not on any account have it supposed that in this
category we class the intelligent Chairman of the Mississippi Committee ; for
he has shown not only that he can reason well himself, but that he posseSBes that
more unusual accomplishment, 11 willingneBB to listen to and be convinced by
the reasons of others. A case from South Carolina, where he handsomely yields
to the argument of Bro. MACKEY, and this from Indiana, where he certainly gives
way some, are evidences that he is not atubborn in his opinions ; and there is a
glimmering of hope, in a portion of his report, that he may yet abandon his
position on the subject of Masonry in New York. And now to return to the
"ancient usages." We have as much veneration for the" land-mark1 which our
fathers have set," and as little desire "to make innovations upon the body of
Masonry," as any of our brethren can possibly evince. But we most modestly
enggest that every custom which a few years have sanctioned, and which relates
only to the local mode of government and to the police regulations of the Order, is not a "land-mark" or a portion of the "body of Masonry." Even if
antiquity is to be considered a sufficient argument in the maintenance of any
Masonic custom, however repugnant to the common sense of the present day,
we are yet to learn that it can properly be offered in the present case. So far
as we can learn, the practice of issuing " Dispensations " to open new Lodges, ail
in use in the United States, is of American origin, and Masonry has not yet become so ancient on this continent, as to authorize the setting up of its usages as
land-marks. It is our impression that in England, the country whence we derive
the " Regulations " by which we profeBB to be governed, such ·instruments are
only issued by the Provincial Grand Master, for a brief period, until the will-of
tbe Grand lllaeter can be ascertained. If· that be favorabe, a Warrant is given
(52]

by him, which fully empowers those to whom it Is granted to do all that a
Lodge of Masone of right may do, and its only qualification is that the next
succeeding Grand Lodge has the power either to confirm or annul it, a l'ower
which, after all, any Grand Lodge has over the charters of all its subordmates
at any time. It would seem then, that if there be "innovation"· any where, it
is not in the addition to the limited privile'ges by some so stoutly maintained as
necessary to the lawfulness of Lodges under dispensation, but is really in that
very limitation itself. The practice is doubtless a good one that Lodges in their
infancy should be more particularly subjected to the scrutiny of the Grand Lodge,
that it may determine by the evidences offered whether the new creation should
be continued in existence. But by whatever name their tenure may be known,
whether Dispensation, Charter or Warrant, we can see no reason and have heard
of no law why they should not be Lodges in fact as well a.~ in name, and while
they exist, do all that 11 regular Lodge Is empowered to do by the ancient laws.
We have once or twice before alluded to this subject in this report, but believe
that we have not made any unnecessary repetition ; and we take the occasion
to say that should nny good reason be presented us for a change of the opinions
WP. now entertain, we will as frankly record such change, as bus our brother of
MiSBiesippl In the South Carolina case.

· Several of the Committees on Foreign Correspondence during the past aud present year, have devoted ~ome space to the discussion of the subject whether reports
ema.nating from such Committees should or should not be adopl.ed by the Grand
Lodge. The first is probn.bly the course most generally pursued-more, doubtless, from force of habit and from courtesy to the writers, than from any partic·
~tar consideration of its J!roprie.ty or impropriety. The Committee of Missouri,
like that of North Carofina, think that" Reports on ~'oreign Correspondence
can have no value, except as the Gmnd Lodge may give by its adoption.~
From this Bro. KrNG dissents, as he considers it "obviously improper for one
Grand Lodge to legislate or adjudicate upon the proceedings of all other Grand
Lodges, as it must do in adopting these reportll." While we do not at all assent to
the assertion of Missouri on the one hand, we do not clearly perceive the force ·
of the argument of New York on the other. That these reports have no
value except such as may be given them by a bare majority of the votes of a Grand
Lodge, we are surprised to hear from one who has earned such celebrity as a
~Iasonic writer, as has Bro. FosTER, of Missouri. Setting ourselves, for the moment, beyond the pale of the discussion, it is usual to commit the preparation of
such pap:rs to the hands of those who arc st~pposed to be the most intelligent
and best mformed among the brethren ; and 1s not the carefully considered and
well digested opinion of five, or three, or even one such, of more real value
than twenty or fifty hasty and inconsiderate votes in opposition, given without
reflection, and founded, perhaps, in ignorance? Would any intelligent Mason
reject the o:pinions of Bro. MooJlE, of Massachusetts, or of Bro. MACKEY, of
South C_arolma, because, perchance, the Grand Lodge of their respective
States might, by a single vote, refuse to adopt a report which embodied them?
Would Bro. FoSTEJl himself, in such a case, think any the. l~ss of his own welld~served i:putation for Masonic skill and ability, ol' be induced to believe that
his own opinions possessed no value ? Probably not. The fact is that those reports are entitled to such consideration as the known reputation or apparent
Masonic intelligence and ability of the authors ma.y justify, whether they are
adopted by a Grand Lodge or not ; and the. vote of a. Grand Lodge is quite as
likely to be erroneous, as the conclusions of such a Mason as ought to be selected to perform a duty so important. Thus much for our opinion that an able report is not altogether valueless, even though it bear not the impress of the
Grand Lodge's formal approbation. On the other hand, we do not see how such
a body " legislates or adjudicates upon the proceedings of all other Grand
Lodges·" by adopting such a report, as Bro. KING declares it does. Such an
a<it is simply an expression of approval of the opinions, conclusions and

In the final report of the Committee on the Condition of Masonry, they sum
up the principal causes for congratulation upon the present prospects of the
Fraternity in the United States, as follows:" 1. The great increase of Lodges.
2. The great increase of membership, both by initiation a.11d affiliation.
3. The liigh character of those who have thus become members.
4. The greater attention to all the practical and moral duties of the Craft, and more
especially in the attendance at the Lodges.
5. The greater study of standard Masonic works, and closer inquiry into the more
hidden mysteries of the Fraternity.''

And upon the other hand they set forth the following aH the principal evils
which threaten danger to the Institution: "I. The great increase of Lodges. (Lodges being too frequently established in localities where they can not permanently flounsh.)
2. The great increase of membership by initiation. (Too little regard being paid to
the requisite inquiries as to the character of the candidate.)
3. The tendency to ostentation and display-making regalia jewels superior to em•
blematic jewels.
4. Tlie keeping too late hours at the Lodge meetings.
5. The haste with which candidates are hurried through the degrees, and the too
frequent applications for dispensations.
6. The carrying of diff'erences of opinion in the 'meetings of our different Masonic
bodies out of doors, and keeping them over night.
7. The want of uniformity of work.
8. The want of firmness m administering discipline for moral delinquency.
9. The shifting of individual duty and responsibility to aBsociated irresponsibility.
And 10. Too much legislation."

These, say the Committee, are presented for the purpose of exciting a spirit
of inquiry among the brethre11 ; and as they are evils which concern not the jurisdiction of New York alone, we set them forth at length as a caution to those
who may need it among ourselves.
We notice a very proper report from the Committee on Grievances. A petitioner set forth that in 1837, he was made a Mason, as he supposes, iu a clandestine Lodge ; that as soon as he was made aware of the fact, he ceased to meet
with them ; that he had since been expelled by that body ; and that he now desired to be healed by being allowed to unite with some Lodge. The Committee
were of the opinion that the Grand Lodge could not properly entertain such a
petition i that it had no cognizance of clandestine Masons ; and that the petitioner, it he desired to be made a Mason, must apply to a subordinate Lodge in
the usual way, by petition, and with the regular initiation fee.

" But, from the well known and universally admitted maxim of 'once a Mason, always
a Mason,' it follows that a demitted brother cannot, by such demission, divest himself of
all his Masonic responsibilities to his brethren, nor be deprived of their correlative respon·
sibility to him. An unaffiliated Mason is still bound by certain obligations, of which he
cannot, under any circumstances, divest himself, and by similar obligations are the Fra·
temity bound to him. It is not permitted here to mention all these obligations in detail,
but I may allude to some of them, such as secrecy, aid in the hour of pressing danger,
and reverence and respect for a brother's family. In relation to those points no unaffi.Ji.
ated Mason can claim exemption, and he has therefore, on the principles of equality, a
right to demand their observance towards himself by others. In conclusion; I may add
that the most bitter denouncer of the practice of demitting cannot, and shall not, go farther than myself in condemning the whole tribe of unaffiliated Masons, as men regardleH
of their duties and unworthy of any other Masonic consideration than that which is ex·
torted by the irresistible force of inalienable vows."

Fellows and by the Church to signify dismission. They conclude with the recommendation that every non-affiliated Mason be summoned on a charge of
unmasonic conduct; that if he fail to appear within a reasonable time, he be
suspended for twelve months ; and that, if at the end of that time he still neglects to present himself or show good cause for his conduct, he be expelled forever. In connection with this subject they propose an alteration of that portion
of the Text-Book which permits a Mason to belong to more than one Lodge at
the same time.
Upon the subject of Petitions the Committee express rurj>TUe to hear" that a
<lustom has obtained to refer them to Committees for investigation and report,"
and they declare it too " monstrous and absurd " to find favor among intelligent
Masons. This certainly takes us not a little aback. Our limited knowledge of
Masonic usage had induced us to suppose that this was the general, if not universal custom, and that its omission, not its practice, should be legitimate cause
for surpise ; and in all our reading and experience we have never before known
the custom to be attacked. But whether it be old or new, we believe it to be
good and necessary, notwithstanding the arguments of our intelligent brethren
of Virginia. They consider it improper thus to place upon two or three the
responsibility of openly reporting unfavorably uron the application of a candidate, and thereby perhaps incurring the ill-will o those who recommended.him;
and they think it is properly the duty of every member of the Lodge to act as a
special Committee in such case, making his report only with his secret ballot.
The old adage that "that which is everybody's business is nobody's," would
probably be as true here as elsewhere, and thus were Committees abolished,
notwithstanding the abstract kuth that every member ought to examine into the
character of the applicant, it is extremely probable that in nine cases out of ten
no such examination would be had at all. As to the fear of responsibility, we
do not think that such an argument was worthy of finding place in such a report.
Cases of Emergency, so called, are discussed at considerable length, and, with
the exception of the applications of military or sea-fa.ring men, in the service of
their country, and therefore not the controllers of their own time and residence,
they discover none which should properly be classed under such a head. " The
ordi.nary excuse of being about to travel to a new home," say they, "is, at this
day, by no means valid· for such has been the appreciation of Masonry by all
civilized countries for the last century, that there is scarce a neighborhood to
be found where there is not a Masonic Lodl!'e. And, looking at the question
through another and equally justifiable medium, it behooves the profane to con·
tribute hi1 feafor initiation to that Lodge from whoae storea he expects to derive iumtance,
if need be." A morsel of good doctrine which we in California, who have been
so overstocked with Atlantic off-hand manufactures, can well appreciate.
The practice of conferring Honorary Membership upon distinguished brethren,
or those who have long and faithfully served the Fraternity, is maintained as
just and 11roper; and it is supported by reference to the case ot' LA FAYETTE, who,
during his last visit to this country, was made an honorary member of many
Lodges, and of one or two Grand Lodges, and to the more recent one of LE
BLilic DE MAR'<ONNAY, who was elected an honorary member of the· Grand
Lodge of Massacbusetts, with the rank of Senwr Grawl, Warden I The Committee
think, however, that the conferring of this honor should not exempt the recipient
from his proper contributions to the Masonic Craft, if his ability will permit
him to present them, nor excuse him from any of the requitements of Masonry.
Upon the subject of Re-instatement, the Committee go into an examination of
the·separa~ questions of membership in the Or4er, and membership of a Lodge,

punished by a forfeiture of the la.st, 'Without loBing his pi>sition in th : first.

the United Grand Lodge of England, and the Grand Lodge of Ireland will respond to our efforts for an interchange of Masonic information. It has seemed
to us a little remarkable that, while the Grand Orients of France and Belgium,
the Grand Lodge of Germ.any and the National Mother Grand Lodge of the
Three Globes in Prussia, have so readily recognized our offers of correspondence,
the Grand Lodges of the United Kingdoms, speaking our own language, and
being, in fact, the Masonic parents of the Institution in America, should have
been so backward in responding to our humble efforts in search of light from
those ancient sources. The increased facilities for communication between the
inhabitants of the Old and New World, which the inventions and improvements
of the past few years have brought about, and the constant communion between
the Masons of the two Hemispheres which has been the consequence, render it
most important that a more general knowledge, both of the local transactions of
the Craft, and of the le~lslation which affects the universal welfare of our An
cient Order on either side of the Atlantic, should be disseminated among the
brethren in Great Britian and America. We are willing to suppose that we are
uot likely to teach them much, but we are ourselves most anxious to learn all
that may be taught by those to whom antiquity has given the right to confer
instruction, and whose duty it is, as Most Excellent Masters, to dispense light
among their leBB informed brethren.

BEl.GIUM.
We acknowledge the receipt from the Grand Secretary of the Grand Orient
of Belgium, of a printed communication accompanying three ordinances of
that body, relative to the establishment and continuance of certain Lodges, the
suspension of several others, and the supp1·ession of one of their standing Regulations. This last is a matter of some importance, as, so far as we understand
its effects, it is intended to throw open in the Lodges the discussion of political
and religious subjects, heretofore forbidden. We have not information enough,
however, in the brief communication sent us, to justify comment. Three subjects are presented by the Grand Orient for the consideration of the brethren
in the Kingdom :
1. By what means can the principles of Free Masonry best be made beneficial
to the world profane?
'
2. Of the indifference existing among Masons ; its causes, character, consequences, and the means of remedying it.
3. Of the education of women, in a Masonic point of view.
Theses upon these 9.uestions appear to be expected from all who may choose
to discuBB them, and directions are given for the manner in which they shall be
prepared and addressed. The Senior Grand Warden, V&RHAEOEN, Senr. presi<led, and L. THEREMIN is Grand Secretary.

The printed transactions of' the Grand Lodge of Germany, for the months of
:\larch, June, September and October, 1854, have been received, together with
its Masonic Calendar for the years 185-l and 1855, containing a complete catalogue of the officers and member~ of that body, and u. list of thl\ Grand and

[74)

The Grand Nations.I Mother Lodge of the Three Globes, which e.lso holds its
Communice.tions in Berlin, age.in fe.vors us with its proceedings. Those before
us are for the months of September, November, e.nd December, 1854, and January, 1855.
The most important matter we note among them is the 11Ction ta.ken npon u.
lnte edict of the Grand Orient of Belgium. This was referred to in our notice
of the proceedings of that body, but the information given in the Arrete sent
us was so meagre, the.t we scarcely comprehended its full meaning. It appears,
however, that the Grand Orient of Belgium has not only repee.led the ordinance
which prohibited the discussion of politico.I and religious questions in the Lodges, - declaring that such a regulation was simply one of expediency and not
necessarily e. fundamental law - but has actually recommended to its subordinates the encouragement of such discussions. To this the Grand Lodge of the
Three Globes gives its most unqualified condemnation; and, letting its action
keep pace with its opinion, by e. une.nimous vote has resolved to cease all communication with the Belgian Grand Orient, e.nd has forbidden the Freemasons
within its jurisdiction to hold any intercourse with those of Belgium, while thi~
doctrine shall preve.il in the Masonic Senate of that Kingdom. A similar rcso·
lution had previously been adopted by the Grand Lodge of Saxony.
At this late period in our report, neither our time nor inclination permits us
to indulge in any extended remarks upon the important question thus presented. The action of the Grand Orient of Belgium strikes us as likely to produce
most pernicious effects upon the Order in that country, and is absolutely in contravention of that which we have supposed to be Me.sonic law. We believe the.t
no subject should ever be mooted in a Lodge of Freemasons, that does not relate to Masonry or to Me.sonic objects. Neither political opinions nor 1·eligious
creeds come within this category, for with neither party nor sect has Masonry
aught to do. Our nearest approach to politics is the requirement that every
life.son shall be a good and peaceable citizen or subject, and obey and support
the laws of the land in which he lives; and the only religion we demand is a
belief and trust in the Almighty God. Within these bounds he may be royalist
or republice.n, protestant or papist, Christian, Jew, or Turk, entertaining any
political opinion or confiding in any particule.r form of religious faith, e.nd still
meet ou the level of equality with his brethren. But for the very reason tlmt
Masonry embraces men of so many different countries, sects, and opinions, the
discussion of subjects upon which such wide and impassable differences must
ever exist, is, and ought to be prohibited in our assemblages- peace and harmony being the absolute essentials for the maintenance of our Order and the fultilment of its charitable and fraternal purposes. We regret, therefore, that our
Belgian brethren have thus invited the introduction of discord where naught
but. harmony should be, but are not prepared to te.ke such u.n extreme step in
regard to them for that reason, ad has the National Mother Grand Lodge in
Prussia.
We notice that an e.mendment to the Constitution of this last has been proposed, by which a member of a Lodge, removing to another place, is not to be
charged with e.n e.ffiliation fee, upon being e.dmitted to membership in another
Lodge under that jurisdiction.

To the M. ·• W:. Grand Master of Masons in California: At the stated meeting of our Lodge, Hawaiian, No. 21, held on the 4th February, 1856, the undersigned were duly appointed a committee to address you, and
o.sk your advice and direction on a matter of vital importance to the peace and
prosperity of the ere.ft on these Islands.
In the performance of this duty we would respectfully represent to you the
following facts : In the year 1843, a Brother named Le Tellier, then commanding a French
whale ship in this ocean, duly empowered by the Grand Council of the 33d of
France to institute Me.sonic Lodges in the Pacific, in places over which no other
jurisdiction had previously been extended, granted a warrant to certain brethren
to open a Lodge in this city under the name of " Le Progrea de L 'OWLnie." For
~ome yea.rs this Lodge prospered and added to its list of members the no.mes of
many of our first and most estimable citizens ; being considered a legitimate
Lodge and legally constituted, which, indeed, it undoubtedly was.
About the year 1850 or 1851, severe.I causes combined to break up the Lodge,
and it ceased to work or to meet ; the warrant lay neglected in the Lodge chest,
and the Lodge was considered extinct. This state of things continued for nearly
two years, when, in 1852, a number of the olcl members of the Lodge " Le
Progrea," together with a few recent comers, met and agreed to ask for the jurisdiction of the State of California over these Islands. For this purpose they applied to the M:. W.·. Grand Lodge of California for a dispensation to open a
Lodge, which was granted, and the followin~ year they received a charter under
the name of Ilawaiian Lodge, No. 21, which is our present flourishing body. At
the time of its formation, the old members, then surviving, of" Le Progrea," formally me.de over the jewels and appurtenances of that Lodge to tae new one,
o.nd themselves became active members, to a man, of Hawaiian Lodge. Thesr.
circumstances we have thought it best to recapitulate, although yon are doubtless already acquainted with them.
Now for the point at issue. About a year ago severe.I members of Hawaiian
Lodge, for reasons best known to themselves, withdrew from that body and, rescuing the old Le Tellier warrant from the oblivion to which it had seemingly
been consigned, organized themselves into a Lodge under it, bearing the old
no.me of" Le Progres· de L'Oceanie." As they did no work at first, but gave out
that they had applied to the proper authorities in France for a new charter, or
an endorsement of the old one, our Lodge continued to regard them with fraternal and kindly feelings. Of late, however, our fears have been excited by the
fact that they have commenced work and conferred degrees on several persons,
Home of whom could not have been received in our Lodge ; and, feeling It our
duty at least to inquire into their authority, our Lodge, at its meeting In January, 1856, appointed a committee to viRit the Lodge "Le Progrh," and examine>
their warrant or charter.
This committee performed the 1luty e.ssigned them, and, at the conclusion of
their examination, presented the following report : " To the W.·.M.·. and Brethren uf Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21 :Two of :your committee presented themselves as visiting brethren at the Lodge door
on an evenmg of meeting of the" Progres de L'Oceanie," and, through the Tyler, asked
admission, requesting, however, that they might first see the charter of the Lod_ge before
entering. After the annoWicement of this reqyest, and some delay, we were mvited to
enter, but without previous exhibition of the charter. This invitation we declined to arcept, upon the ground that we could not salute the chair Wilcss we knew the assemblagt'
to be a duly constituted Lodge. After some further delay the door was thrown open to
us, and we were informed that the so-called Lodge was at refreshment, and we could thus
see what we desired.
The brother who wore the jewel of Master (R. G. Davis) then exhibited to us a roll of
documents, and accompanied and followed this exhibition with sundry explanation~. Thr
documents were in French, and were translated at the time in whole, and mostly nloud ,
hy Bro. Guillou, one of your committee. They consisted of the following:A paper empowering one Brother Le Tellier to establish, under authority and jurisdir.

It commenced b:y acknowledging the receipt of a communication ( planchi) addressed
to the Most W orsh1pful Grand Master of the Grand Orient of France, and then proceeded
as follows : 'The Grand Orient would be gratified to add another subordinate Lodge to its jurisdiction. But the warrant of constitution (le pollOOir constitutif), of which you have sent

in France. There exists in France another Masonic power which has created your craft.
(cree votre metier.) We have therefore thought it our duty to give no sequence to your

Bro. Davis mformed us that several documents bad been from time to time received
from the Supreme Council, and that in them all the legality of the existence of " Le
Progres de L'Oceo.nie" as a Lodge, was recognized either expressly or by implication.
But all these p,apers were understood to be of date prior to the suspension of work by
" Le Progrt!s, ' and they were not asked for by your committee because they seemed to
ha".e _no be~ring- upon that which your committee considered to be the special object of
their mvest1gat1on namely :Whether after the prolonged suspension of all work, and of active existence as a corporate body 1 the " Progres ik L' Oceo.nie" still preserved its original powers as a Lodge ;
and whether those J>?Wers w~re_ retained by a sp~cijic permission from its parent, or oy
means of a general hcense ex1stmg under the domm10n of that parent, by which a subordinate Lodge could resume work of its own impulse, after a dormancy of indefinite dura·
tion ; or if any limit existed, then what was that limit.
No limit of time, or special permission for resumption was shown to us, or contended
for as existing; on the contrary, the resumption of work was justified by a general law or
rule of the French Masonic authorities, permitting or at least toleratmg, resumption of
full life and powers after any suspension, however long, provided that in the interim neither the charter had been returned to its parent by the subordinate Lodge, nor had been
taken from the latter by its parent, nor publicly declared among the brethren to be forfeited.
.
Neither of these bars is supposed to exist in the case of the" Progres de L'Oceanie."
The existence of such a general law or rule in the French jurisdiction was confidently asserted b:y Bro. Davis; but upon inquiry from us, he showed us neither printed nor written
recogniuon, by persons of apparent Masonic authority and high standing, of either law
rule, or usage to such effect. He stated, in reply to our inquiry, that after consultatio~
with some of the brethren of "Le ProJ!:T"fs,' 1 they had decided that the papers already exhibited to us were, in their opinion, air that courtesy or Masonic fellowsnip required of
them to show us. But we asked further of Bro. Davis whether among the papers in his
possession, as a Brother Mason, there were any documents from the Supreme Council of
aate subsequent to the receipt of knowledr,c by that Council of the long dormancy i:nd
spontaneous revival of the " Pro!!T!• de L Oceanie ;" and if so, whether he was willing to
inform us how the acts of that boCly were regarded by its constituting parent 1
No such letters or papers were shown us, and we were left to conclude that none such
had been receivedi ancf that no sign of recognition had been obtained since the resumption of work by "Le Progres."
How far this state of things might depend upon usage, under the Scottish rite in general, or the French jurisdiction in particular; or how far it might depend upon want of

punctuality on the part of the Supreme Council or o~ the S_ubordinate Soc!ety, w~ had no
means of ascertaimng. And although such infor!l'all.on might have been mterestmg, and
indirectly useful, we did not feel clearly bow f~r it.might be .decorous to urgi; suc.b questions involving the internal discipline of orgamzat1ons to which we were foreign.
W~ therefore ceased our inquiries here, and now beg leave to report, as above stand•
narrated.
Respectfully,

Your committee tind that the book8 uf these Lodges i;enerally, have been
kept in 11 neat and orderly manner, but they observe a few cases where the Secretaries have not been sufficiently explicit in matters of importance, while their
records are sometimes blemished with useless repetitions, inappropriate language, and superfluous and improper entries.
While gratified to find that so much Masonic skill and experience are exhibited in the work and records of most of the Lodges, your committee are compelled to notice a few exceptions, where a want of such experience is strongly
indicated. In some instances Lodges have not been closed from one regular
meeting to another, but have been called off for several successive meetings.
In some cases too much work bas been done at one meeting;- business bas been
done in the lower degrees which belonged only to the higher; and work bas
been done in the higher degrees which should have been done in the lower.
The records of Mountain Lodge, in several instances, do not show the names
of the officers and members present, nor that the Lodge was duly opened, or the
business properly transacted ; and it is necessary to say that the books of that
Lodge have been very badly kept.
The records of Umty Lodge show that petitions for initiation WP.re received
and referred on the 15th and 18th of the same month. They also show that
examinations as to qualification in the second degree, were bad in a Master's
Lodge ; anil the records generally are badly kept.
;.. The records of Clay Lodge show that petition8 were received and referred,
without stating whether they were for initiation or affiliation ; and that the
Lodge was sometimes opened in the first d~ree, and then work done in those
above, without any further opening of the Lodges. In some cases, too, no report
of a committee appeared, before the ballot for a candidate was bad.
Your committee are convinced that the errors above alluded to, were the
results only of a want of Masonic instruction and experience, and not of any
intention to violate the ancient usages of Masonry, or the Constitution and re.gulations of this Grand Lodge ; and believing that the foregoing statement w!ll

Bro: C. R. Saunders, from the same committee, presented the following report: To the M:. W:. Gmnd Lodge of Oalifornia : Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Jesse Morrill, from the
sentence of expulsion by Washington Lodge, No. 20, on the 22d day of June, A. L.
5854, beg leave to report: That they have examined what purports to be a.
transcript of the proceedings in this case, and are unable to find from said
papers - 1st, What wer~ the charges preferred against said Morrill. 2d, That
he was ever notified to attend at the special Communication at which he was
expelled. 3d, From an examination of the evidence transmitted to this Grand
Lodge, we think that hearsay and irrelevant evidence was admitted. 4th, The
vote upon bis expulsion was improperly had. 5th, The vote of each member
was not recorded as required by the rules of the Grand Lodge. 6th, 'l'he record
does not show that two thirds voted for his expulsion. In short, we find that
nearly all the proceedings had against him were conducted without regard to
the regulations governing trials, as adopted by this Grand Lodge at its Annual
Communication, in May, 1854; and it appears from the records sent up that
there have already been three trials for the same offence. Your.committee also
find that this matter was presented to the Grand Lodge at its last session, when
a decision in regard to it W!l-S postponed until this Communication ; and, in the
meantime, the sentence of expulsion was continued in force. They also find among
the papers transmitted to them, a petition signed by fifty-six members of said
Lodge, (No. 20,) recommending that the sentence of expulsion be reversed, and
that the said Jesse Morrill be restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry. In view, therefore, of all the facts and circumstances - of the irregularity
of the trial - of the long time during which he has labored under sentence of
expulsion- and of the earnest recommendation of so many members of the
Lodge which expelled him that he be restored, we recommend the propriety of
reversing the decision of Washington Lodge, No. 20, and restoring the appellant
to all the rights and privileges of Masonry, and for that purpose we offer the
following resolutions:Resolued, That the sentence of expulsion heretofore passed against Jesse Morrill, by
Wa.vhington Lodge, No. 20, be 8J1nulled, and the said Jesse Morrill be restored to all the
rights and privileges of Masonry.
·

resolution to Bro. Jesse Morrill, under se,al of the Grand Lodge.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
C. R. SAUNDERS, Oltairman.
