Bro. R. E. Cole, from the Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence, appointed
at the last Communie t1011, presented the following report: To the JI[:. W. •. Grand Lodge of California : Your committee on Masonic Jurii:;iprudence, appointed at the last Communication, to whom was referred certain portions of the 111:. W.·.Grand Master:s Acl[99]

330

331

dress, delivered at that time, respectfully report; tha.t, owing to the late period
of the session when they were appointed (it being the last day) they were unable
to make any report at that time, and they would hardly feel authorized to do so
·at this late date, were the subjects referred to of mere ordinary import. But
being desirous that the very excellent sentiments and recommendations contained in that Address should none of them pass unnoticed, but ·receive the sanction and hearty approval of this Grand Lodge-breathing, as they do, those
pure principles of our time-honored and beloved Order, which cannot be too
freely promulgated - your committee would submit the following for your consideration and approval.
For those portions which advert to the government of Lodges and the proper
deportment of their members, and to the manner in which the opening and closmg
ceremonies should be conducted, your committee would bespeak a thorough and
careful perusal by all members of Lodges, and by their officers in particular ; as
they contain most excellent and timely suggestions, as well as sound masonic doctrines and principles, which ought to be strictly observed by every Mason.
That portion which refers to the so-called "side degrees," your committee
conceive to be treated of in the true light, and they concur with the Grand
Master in the opinion that we cannot with propriety legislate upon a subject so
entirely foreign to our organization, and one over which we can have no control.
In reference to the non-payment of dues by members of Lodges, your committee would recommend Lodges to enforce most rigidly Sec. 9, of' Article X. of
the Constitution of this Grand Lodge ; for the non-payment of the regular dues
by members when they are able to comply with that requisition, would seem to
indicate that there was a want of that high standard of moral integrity which
should predominate in the breast of every Mason; and if any will thus easily cut
themselves off from membership, their loss will undoubtedly be advantageous to
the Lodge.
- .
That portion relative to the too rapid advancement of candidates, and to carelessness in regard to their qualifications, your committee think fully provided
for in the 13th standing resolution of this Grand Lodge ; and would Lodges adhere to it in · its spirit and intent, there could be no cause of complaint in that
respect.
That portion which relates to the making of Masons in one jurisdiction, of persons residing in another, your committee conceive to be fully provided for in
the 50th standing resolution of this Grand Lodge, passed at its last session, an<l
since (it is proper to say) the Address under consideration was presented.
With that portion alluding to profane swearing, intemperance and gaming,
your committee most heartily concur; but they conceive that the entire teachings and principles of our beloved Order'!l.re so utterly averse to the evils in
question, that they deem any special legislation on the subject altogether super/
fluous.
On the subject of Lodges of Instruction, your committee concur in the recommendation, and would commend for it an earnest consideration by all mell\bers
of Lodges in the jurisdiction; and, when practicable, would advocate their establishment under special dispensations.
In reference to Lodge libraries, yo~r committee can conceive of no better
means for diffusing pure masonic light and knowledge than by their establishment, and the judicious selection of such books as will tend to enlight~n and ennoble the mind. They therefore would earnestly commend the subJect to the
attention of every Lodge.
With the views of the Grand Master, on the subject of non-affiliated
)fasons, your committee entirely agree, and they conceive that the present
StandinO' Resolutions relative thereto do not meet the subject correctly. They
would r~commend, therefore, the rescinding of the resolutions numbered 12, 44,
and 46, and in place thereof propose the following, which, in their opinion, will
better serve the end in view : -

, To the M.·. W.·. Grand Lodge of California : Your committee, to whom was referred the application of 11fountain Lodge, U.
D., for a remission of dues and charter fee, if one be granted, submit the following report : · The grounds upon which this petition is based, are, that the expenses of building have entailed upon them heavy debts, while at the same time they have
" made but eight Master Masons " during the year past.
Your committee reluctantly refer to this application as an illustration of
those insidious dangers to which our M.·. W. ·• Grand Master bas so frequently
called our attention. We mean bis warning against an injudicious desire to accumulate Lodges, or to hurriedly and incautiously extend the membership of
our noble fraternity.
Now, it seems to your committee that a Lodge under dispensation is in such a
peculiarly inchoate condition of existence as to imggest the necessity of infinite
care in all steps that tend to the incurment ofheavy liabilities. For, in the first
place, it must be remembered that there is no positive assurance that a Lodge
under dispensation can obtain a charter at all ; and if obtained, your committee
are of the opinion that it is an instrument too sacred and important in its character to be made at once the subject of serious and embarrassing liabilities.
In this case, the petition is for the remission of dues, which are known and
defined, and a contingent petition for the remission of charter fee, should a
charter be granted.
Your committee cannot recommend the granting of the requests made, and
will take the present opportunity of exprelllling what will be their rule of action
in these cases of the remission of dues.
Where the embarrassments of a Lodge, upon which a petition for the remission of dues is made, are the result of those providential injuries or destruction
to property over which the members of Lodges cannot exercise any control, then
your committee will most cheerfully recommend that assistance which it is peculiarly the province of Grand Lodges to afford. But in cases where liabilities
have been voluntarily and deliberately incurred, your committee cannot conceive it to be the duty of this Grand Lodge to step in and render that kind of
assistance which must come finally from the subordinate Lodges, who are inflicting upon themselves the inconvenience and restraints of a more stringent and
rigid economy. Let this Grand Lodge begin to award favorable responses to
such petitions for relief as those necessarily embraced in the above category, and
in five years it will become itself a petitioner, or the paralyzed supporter of a
mass of impudent legal liabilities.
These remarks your committee feel called upon to make with regard to the
genera.I principles involved in their duties, and with an earnest desire that they
will not be offensive, or made the subject of a perverted construction.
With respect to the foregoing application, your committee offer the following
resolution : &solved, That Mountain Lodge be granted twelve months' time for the paymeut of
its dues and charter fee.
·
All of which is respectfully submitted.
JOHN F. MOR8E, }
CHARLE8 MARSH,
Chm111i/Ue,
J. A. JACISON,

Bro. W. M. Stafford, from the same committee, also presented the following report: To the M:. W. ·. Grand Lodge of California: Your committee, to whom was referred the papers from El Drnado Lodge, No.
26, praying the Grand Lodge to reinstate A. Haas in the rights and privileges of
Masonry, and to membership i11 that Lodge, from which he had been expelled,
beg leave to report : - That in the opinion of your committee the Grand Lodge
has the right to restore an expelled Mason to all the rights and privileges of
Masonry, upon a proper application from the Lodge by which he was expelled;
but they deny the right of' the Grand Lodge to restore him to membership in I\
particular Lodge without the unanimous consent of the members of' that Lodge.
His being reinstated in all the rights and privileges of Masonry, in the opinion
of your committee, places him in the position of a non-affiliated Mason. They
recommend the restoration of Mr. Haas, and for that purpose offer the following
resolution: Resolved That A, Haas, heretofore expelled by El Drnado Lodge, No. 26, be re·•tored to ail1 the rights and privileges of Masonry.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

Bro. H. H. Hartley, from the Committee on Education, preseuted the following report:....:.
1b tlte lrl.-. W.-. Grand Lodge of California : The Committee on Education, appointed at the present Communication, cannot
petmit the same to expire without presenting a short report upon this important
Rnd Interesting subject. Your committee are gratified to learn, from comµmnication wlih the representatives of the several Lodges, that this branch of MR·
Ronic charity has received from the fraternity that zealous carr. and attention
which its importance demands. We congratiilate ourselves that but very f'ew
orphans claim our fostering protection, and that those who are so unfortunate
1\8 to be In that distressing position, fully realize from the protecting influence
of our Order, that, in the bosom of tho MMonic family, they may find some of
the lost blessings and protection of home.
The propriety of endowing and erecting Masonic schools or colleges, bas been
frequently commented upon in connection with the subject of Masonic educa-·
tion, and by some the advantages of such R system has been strongly urged, and
the advocates thereof point with pride and pleasure to the map:niflcent and philanthropic institutions of Continental Europe, erected by zealous Mason~, RUpported by an ardent brotherhood, and devoted to the glorious cause of developing the mind and Intellect of the rising youth of our Order. Ilut while we, no
leRB than the7, appreciate the Importance of their labors, admire the genius of
their lnsiitnt1ons, rmd praise the ardor wlt.h which their almost herculean taskR
are accomplished, still have we renaon to congrat11.late ourselves that under the
genius of the watchful and provident institutions under which we live, our duties upon this head are comparatively trifling. The importance, nay, the almost
indillJlenaab!llty of education, has so impressed itself upon the minds of our
statesmen and law-makers, that it has Rlmoat become 11 Mered cbnrge and truRt
•The return• for Luington Lodge have l'ince heen received.

[112]

in their bands, and but in few States in our confederation can even the poorest
and most destitute complain of inability to obtain this great boon. State vies
with State, and legislator with legislator, In endeavoring most favorably to extend to all, freely and abundantly, this glorious privilege. Our
adopted State is not behind the rest; gradually but surely is she perfecting a
thorough system of general education, and the quiet village school-house now
dots the plains and springs into existence in the gorges of the mountains, where
but a few years past all was quiet aud tranquility. While such a system as this
prevails, while such a general interest is manifested upon the subject, individual
exertion rarely finds scope for action ; for all enter freely and voluntarily into
the field na co-laborers and co-workers. In this the comparative infancy of
our State, with but a very limited number even of the youth of our Order, and
more especially but few who would require undivided care and attention at our
hands, we would deem it impolitic and Improvident to endeavor to e8tablish any
peculiar, special Masonic education, or endow or establish any school or schools
exclusively for the children of Masons. The different Lodgee throughout the
jurisdiction, we are satisfied, fully alive to the sacred task-nay, the solemn
duty, which becomes a gratifying privilege, that of developing the mind and intellect of those entrusted by circumstances to their charge-do not ne~lect what
they owe to themselves and to the ere.ft, and embrace every opportumty offered
them, with zeal and fidelity.
In their hands, then1 are we for the present content to leave this portion of the
great work· in their cnarge do we confide the watching, the dawning and bringing into existence, and culiivatlon of the minds of our youth. We pray them
faithfully to guard the precious talent committed to their ca1·e, so that they may
ever be ready to render a just and satisfactory account of their stewardship.
Your committee, in conclusion, beg lenvc to offer the following resolutions:
&solved, That this Grand Lodge, in the most solemn manner possible desires to im·
press upon the subordinate Lodges the urgent necessity which exists that the benefits and
privileges of education, in its fullest an<I most perfect manner, should be a1forded to the
ehildreu of all Masons, and more particulnrly to those who by bereavement of parents more
cspeeially are confided to our care and guardian•hip.
& solutd. That each subordinate Lodge, with its annual returns, shall forward to the
Grand Lod!\"e, a statement of all orphans or children of Masons under their care and pro·
tcctiou; particularly setting forth the measures heing taken to supply them with the means
of receiving a proper education.
.

All of which is respectfully submitted.
HENltY H. HARTI,EY, Oltairman.

Bro. H. H. Hartley, from the Committee on Grievances, presented the
following report : To the M. ·. W.-. Grand Lodge of California : The Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred the papers and correspondence relative to the late Padfic Lodge, U. D., at Valparaiso, heretofore under the jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge, report as follows : We find that at the session of the Grand Lodge in 1853, a dispensation was
granted to certain brethren at Valparaiso, Chile, to open a Lodge to be called
Pacifo: Lodge. No further mention of this Lodge appears upon the proceedings
of the Grand Lodge, until the session of 1854, when we find a report from the
then Grand Seeretary, our lamented brother, Levi Stowell, commenting in
rather severe and harsh terms upon the action of said Lodge, in having returned
her dispensation, dissolved the Lodge, and taken a new dispensation from the
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts ; alleging, also, that said Lodge had acted in bad
faith towards this Grand Lodge, and hoping that the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts would revoke their dispensation ; and requiring that the jewels, furniture,
etc., etc., of that Lodge should be forwarded to this Grand Lodge. On the
presentation of this report, the Grand Lodge adopted a resolution soliciting the
Grand Lodge of Massachusetts to instruct Pacific Lodge to comply with our Constitution touching its dissolving its allegiance to this Grand Lodge. Pacific
Lodge has furnished to this Grand Lodge dup}icates of its correspondence with
the Grand Secretar7, from which we perceive that t his Grand Lodge, at its session of 1854, did iOJustice to that Lodge. Application was .made by it for a dispensation a long time before one was granted, and so much delay occurred in
obtaining it that another application was made to the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts for a similar instrument. The dispensation from this Grand Lodge,
however, reached them first, and a Lodge was instituted under it· subsequently,
difficulties having arisen in the Lodge, and another dispensation having reached
the applicants from the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, more liberal in its terms
and giving greater facilities to the members of the Lodge, the brethren, several
of whom hailed previously from that jurisdiction, and who were familiar with its
work and ritual, decided to relinquish the dispensation held by them from this
Grand Lodge ·\which they accordingly did, and a l>ort1on of the members of the
old Lodge coa esced with other Masons and established a new Lodge under the
dispensation from Massachusetts. This course we do not think was Improper or
in violation of Masonic usage or duty, as we have every reason to believe that
Pacific Lodge, while under dispensation from this Grand Lodge, paid o.ll the
dues and charges owing to this Grand Lodge, nnd probably more than was actually due. The entire correspondence of the late Secretary of that Lodge, Bro.
C. T. Ward, Jr., is fraternal and courteous, and in behalf of that Lod~e exhibits
towards this Grand Lodge the proper Masonic spirit. It seems to assign principally as the cause of the dissolution of the connection between thnt Lodge and
this Grand body, the difficulty of obtaining information from it, the
want of knowledge of its work and ritual, and the superior privileges afforded
to them by the dispensation from the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts. These reasons your committee consider to be cogent and deserving of consideration, and
to be a justification of the course taken by said Lodge.
Your committee are further of the opinion that it is unnecessary to require the
late Pacifo: Lodge to forward to this Grand Lodge its furniture, jewels, etc., as
[115]

Bro. J. F. Morse, from the Special Committee appointed at the last Annual
Communication, to whom was referred that portion of the Grand Master's
Address at that time, relative to the subject of a Masonic Hall and Hospital, presented the following report: To the M." W:. &and Lodge of California: Your committee, to whom was referred the subject of a Masonic Hall and
Hospital, submit the following report: After duly considering the subject, they have come to the ensuing conclusions. In their opinion, it is not in any way expedient for this Grand Lodge to involve itself in the expense and anxiety necessarily incurred in such a heavy a.nd
responsible undert11king, as the founding and maint11ining of a Masonic Hospi·
tal. We believe it much more judicious for our Fraternity throughout its membership, to take especial interest as citizens, in those State and County hospitals,
the object of which is to meet all those demands for relief which suggests the
establishment of a special Masonic charity,
With regard to the erection of a Masonic Hall, your committee arc averse to
any immediate attempt to fulfil the natural desires of the Fraternity in that particular. We believe it to be a very becoming design, and one worthy of the Grand
Lodge, to accommodate itself with a permanent, comfortable and beautiful
home, in which to hold its Communications, and from which to dispense its authority and benefactions, whenever our circumstances give us the necessary encouragement to do so.
Hence, your committee would suggest the following resolutions: Resolved, That this Grand Lodge shall continue such a standard of revenue as experience will show will afford an annual balance of at least :1111,000 P.xcess of revenue over
expenditures; and that said excess, more or less, be set asicfe annually as an accumulatinf
fund, for the erection of a Masonic Hall.
Resolved, That this Grand Lodge elect at each Annual Communication, a Board of
Trustees. consisting of three members of the aforesaid Grand Body, whose duty it shall
be to judiciously invest all moneys set aside for such accumulating fund, at such interest
as can be obtained without hazard; and that the accruing interest shall be, as fast as possible, added to the principal, and s1milarly invested.
Resolved, That the members of this Board of Trustees shall severally execute and
file bonds, approved by the M.-. W.-. Grand Master, R ... W.-. Grand Secretary, an<! R"
[116)

Which report was received and concurred in; the resolutions were adopted;

sented the following report: [120)

To the M.-. W:.GTand Lodge qf California: Yonr committee, to whom was referred the communication from Ha10aiia11
Lodge, No. 21, at Honolulu, in the Sandwich Islands, setting forth the action
which that Lodge bad taken in respect to ·the so-called Lodge, " Le P1·ogrea de
L'Oce.anie," at that place, and asking the advice of this Grand Lodge in reference
• thereto, beg leave to submit the following : The communication referred to was evidently prepared with much care, and
is characterized by such a spirit of :Masonic courtesy and fraternal forbearance
in regard to those towards whom a feeling of duty compelled the members of
Hawaiian Lodge reluctantly to place tbemoelvcs in· a position of antagonism,
that your committee cannot for a moment doubt the propriety of assuming its
~tatements to be, in all respects correct. With this assumption, the only question propounded in that communication which it is necessary to determine, is,
whether a Lodge-which had for several years ceased to work or to meet-the
members of which, "to a man," bad joined in procuring a charter for another
Lodge, or bad affiliated with that new Lodge after it bad been established-and
the jewels, furniture, and fixtures of which bad, by its old members, unanimou$ly
heen turned over to the new Lodge, which they bad joined in ereatingt.bus being by all its previous members o.bsolutely and unqualifiedly declared extinct--Oould be revived and spring again into legal exi8tcnce by any
power other than that of the Grand liody which first create<! it?
Your committee are of the opinion that the usage of most, if not all, of the
Grand Lodges of the United States would sanction the suggestion, that, where
a Lodge bad for many years lain dormant, hacl failed to meet or perform any of
the duties or functions for which it was established, and bad thus, in effect, violated the implied contract under which it was created, even though its members
might still nominally have their names retained upon its rolls, its chnrter might
justly be declared to be forfeited, and its name blotted out from the register of
Mo.sonic Lodges. Your committee, however, are not forgetful of the fact that the
nsage which might govern in such a ease among the Grand Lodges of America,
may not be the rule of !lCtion in the Grand Body whence the authority to institute the Lodge, "Le I'1·ogrt& de L'Oceanic," first emanated. Of the laws in thi~
respect which arc acknowledged by the Grand Orient of Fro.nee, (which is the Supreme Head of Symbolic Masonry in that empire) or by the '·Grand Council of
the 33d," your committee confess themselves entirely ignorant; and yet it woul<l
be by those laws only, whatever they may be, that the Lodge, "Le Progrea de
UOceanie" should be judged, were.it within the purview of the hypothesis stated
by your committee.
Such, however, docs not appear to be the fact. That Lodge did not simply
remain dormant and inactive, with its list of membership remaining unaltered ;
but all iU member& left it and enrolled their names under !lnother organization.
held under authority from a tlifferent jurisdiction. It would be an absurdity to
assert that a Lodge can exist without a single member upon its register ; and
thus the Lodge, "Le I'rog~a de L'Oceanie" conld not be considered even as a dor·
mant Lodge, it having absolutely committed n political ~uicide, and ceased to
exist by its own voluntary and unanimous act. lts existence thus having terminated, no power other than that of a Grand Lodge could revive it ; and tbu~
far it does not appear that any such exercise of power has been successfully in·
rnked.
Your committee, therefore, not only approve the cm1rse which bas been pursued by Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21, but take the occasion to express their admiration of the Masonic ability and zeal evinced in its action, as well as of the fraternal consideration and neighborly forbearance exhibited under these unfortunate circumstances toward their misguided brethren of the so-called Lo<lge
" Le I'rogi8 de l' Oceanie."
They recommend the adoption of the following resolution: Ruollled, That this Grand Lodge approves I.he action of Hawaiian Lodge, No. ::!J ,
relative to the organization at Honolulu, known as the Lodge" I.e Progh de l' Oreanit ,"

Bro. J. F. Morse, from the Special Committee upon the Revision of the
Standing Resolutions of the Grand Lodge,, presented the following report : To the M. •• W. ·. Grand Lodge of CalifrYrnia : The committee to whom was referred the duty of revising the Standing Resolutions, would respectfully submit, that upon investigating tl1e duty assigned
them, at the late hour at which they received their commission, they found that it
would b1,1 impossible to attend to the same 11s it should be done. While your
committee are unanimous in the opinion that the object in the avpointment of the
committee is one which demands attention, they cannot profitably enter upon
the work without sufficient time to faithfully and carefully elaborate the subjects
8ubmitted.
We would therefore recommend that a committee be appointed at this Communication, whose duty it shall be, during the recess of this Grand Lodge, to
prepare, and present at our next Annual Communication, a carefully digested
plan of condensation of said Resolutions, for the consideration of this Grand
Body.
In addition to the forel(oing, your committee have bad before them several
resolutions referred to them by tllis Grand Lodge, relative to which they present
the following opinions : The resolution offered yesterday morning as a sub8titute for the 2ith Standing
Resolution. is not regarded as an improvement upon that which it is intended to
displace; and your committee recommend that it be .not adopted.
The resolution offered at the same session, to repeal the 57th• Standing Resolution, it is considered inexpedient to concur in ; and they recommend
that that, too, be not adopted.
The resolution offered at the same session, requiring the Secretaries of Lodges
to communicate to all the Lodges within the jurisdiction, the names of all members stricken from the roll for non-payment of duer., is considered as tl'' 'lecessary, inaEmuch as the intention of the resolution i~ evidently meant tv .;c,cx-

[126]

pressed in Section 15, Article X., of the Constitution. Your committee recommend, therefore, that it be not adopted.
The resolution offered at the same session, relative to the i6sue of dispensations for the opening of new Lodges, is also regarded as unnecessary-the 28th
Standing Resolution sufficiently providing for the object therein desired. It is
therefore recommended that it •be not adopted.
The resolution offered at the same session, relative to objections made to the
initiation or advancement of a candidate after election, your committee think
may be sufficiently expressed by the following proposed addition to the 40th
Standing Resolution : " And that wh·en objection is made before the initiation, passin~ or raising of a candi<late, his petition shall be recommitted to a committee, and be subject to a second invest·
igation."

They recommend, thel·efore, that the resolution be not adopted, and that the
amendment above suggested be approved.
The resolutjon requiring the Grand Lecturer to exemplify the work on the
second day of each Communication, your committee consider inexpedient, inasmuch as it should be left to each successive convocation of the Grand Lodge to
prescribe the order of its business.
In conclusion, your committee beg leave to submit the following resolution : Resofoed, That any Lod~e within this jurisdiction which shall receive a brother into
membership without a certilicate of freedom from indebtedness lo the Lodge of which he
was last a member, shall become responsible lo such Lodge for any dues it may have
against him.

All of which is respectfully submitted.
JOHN 1<'. MoRsE, Chairman.

adversely to were rejected; the amendment and resolution recommended
were adopted, and the committee were discharged.

York, inviting an interchange of representatives with this Grand body, would
respectfully report ; that while they belleve that by this mode of int~rcourse

Bro. N. G. Curtis, from the Special Committee to whom was referred the
communication from the Grand Lodge of Canada, announcing its independent organization, and requesting a reciprocation of fraternal regard with this
Grand Lodge, presented the following report: To the M. ·. W. ·. Grand Lodge qf Ca/,ifornia : Your committee, to whom was referred the communication from the new
Grand Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons of Canada, have given the
subject that calm, deliberate and dispassionate consideration which its importance demands ; and they find, from the document ary evidence before them,
wherein is set forth the causes which impelled them to the separation, that
they have severed the link which has so long bound them to their parent Grand
Lodges of Great Britain, and have, in the most solemn manner, assumed the
powers of a separate and independent organization ; and now, extending to this
Grand Lodge, in the name of our divine art, the right hand of brotherhood,•
they confidently claim from us the reciprocation of our fraternal regard.
It has long been a source of sorrow to our Canadian brethren, that the prosperity of the craft in that noble province bas not been commensurate with the rapid
improvement which marked every other branch of social and polltlcal economy.
Their failure to realize that progress in the art which has attended r egular
Lodges in other countries, is mainly attributable to the following alleged grievances:The want of harmony in action and in working, resulting from Lodges hailing
from the Grand Lodges of different countries, perpetuating local and national
feelings and ~rejudices and conflicting interests, and the consequent estrangement of Rffect1on among the brethren of an Order that knows no country, and is
confined to no race : The manifest injustice of Lodges in Canada being required, out of their limited means, to contribute to the accumulated funds of the Grand Lodges of
Great Britain, in addition to havin~ to support their Provincial Grand Lodges,
and especially as a greater proportion of the claims for Masonic assistance are
made by Masons emigrating from the mother country, whilst instances of Masons
leaving Canada for Great Britain in a position to require relief are rare, if they
ever occur at all. The Grand Lodges of Great Britain thus doubly tax the fraternity in Canada, by transfcr}ing to their shores numberless .claimants for Ma8ouic benevolence, at the Rnme tirue that they are receiviag from the Canadian
brethren a large portion of their means of affording that assistllilce : The great inconvenience consequ~nt upon the distance between the mother
Grand Lodges in Great Britain, and the subordinates in Canada;[131]

•

363

362
The appointment of Provincial Grand Masters by the Grand Master of Eng·
land, who, at a distance of four thousand miles, may reasonably be supposed to
be practically ignorant of the social position and requirements of the craft in
Canada • and the nominations of the Provincial Grand Officers by the Provincial
Grand Masters, made, as they are, without reference to the opinions or wishes of
the governed.
The Provincial Grand Lodges, thus constituted, are placed in the equivocal
position of being irresponsible to and independent of the craft in Canada.
We also find, from the record before us, that the Ma.sons of Canada have repeatedly petitioned th~ Grand Lodge of England to remedy the evils here complained of; and that their repeated prayers have been treated with cold indifference and neglect. Finding that the interests of the craft iu the Province
were suffering with increa.eed severity from the causes of which they had complained, feeling deeply the discourteous neglect they had experienced from
the officers of the Grand Lodge of England, and believing it impossible to obtain
those concessions which their position rendered indispensable, it was determined to call a meeting of delegates from all the Canadian Lodges, to consider
the expediency of establishing an independent Masonic Government.
In conformity with that determination, aud in pursuance of a summon~ issued
to a.II the Lodges in Canada, the representatives of forty-one Lodges, hailing
from the Grand Lodges of England, Ireland and Scotland, assembled in the City
of Hamilton, on the 10th day of October, 1855, and in the most solemn manner
passed the following
HESOLlll'IONS :

All of which is respectfully submitted.

From the foregoing statements it would seem that the Grand Lodge of England-a body to which no lover of our holy Order can look without the deepe8t
veneration-the medium through which has flowed all the Masonic light which
now blesses a world-the most magnificent combination of the work of the old
Masters-an institution which, in 1717, established the great landmarks and fixed
• unalterably the true principles of the craft, and elected Anthony Sayer its first
Grand Master, and bas been presided over by the brightest intellects of the realm
down to that bright light in Masonry, the Earl of Zetland, the present Grand Master-has not treated the continued supplications of those who only asked what
was reasonable and just, with that respect and maternal regard which was to have
been expected from her exalted position and distinguished reputation.
Yet, the statements before us being purely exparte, a.re not regarded by your
committee as a sufficient ground for definite action at the present time, on the
part of this Grand Lodge. Thus, while we extend to our aggrieved brethren in
Canada all the sympathy which taxation without repre~entation, inconvenience
without recompense, and petitions treated with coldness and neglect, are calculated to excite-while we would extend to them the hand of fraternal affection,
and desire to be regarded as their true Masonic brethren and co-workers-while
we will ever be ready to come to their lll!sista.nce in the great struggle of mind
with mind in the discussion of those important questions which can only be
settled by such a course-and while we would fondly hope for the time speedily
to arrive when. their brightest hopes and anticipations will be realized, we are
compelled to defer a formal recognition of the body thus created, until future
developments shall make that duty more plain and imperative.
Althou~h compelled, with painful reluctance, to adopt this course, we arc
cheered with the sincere hope that before our next Annual Communication all
their difficulties will have been fraternally settled, and the Grand Lodge of C1mada. found in the great constellation of Grand Lodges of the Universe, receiving
from and returning to the others, rays of ever growing brilliance; which will

ARTICLE IV.
EIECTION OF GRAKD OFFICERS.
SECTION 1. The Most Worshipful ·Grand Master, Right Worshipful Deputy

of its sitting, and shall hold their resper.tive offices until their successors are
duly elected and installed. A majority of all the votes cast at an election for
Grand Officers, shall be necessary for a choice.' All other Grand Officers shall
he appointed in such manner as the Grand Lodge may direct.

the Worshipful Master named in said petition is fully competent to confer the
three degrees of Masonry.

11 written message, therein detailing an account of his official acts during the recess, and the state and condition of Masonry in his jurisdiction ; and shall recommend to the Grand Lodge such measures as he may deem expedient and necessary.

VOTING.

right, shall be entitled to more than one vote.
Ssc. 2. In all questions except those decided by ballot, in the event of n tie,
the presiding officer shall have the casting vote.
Sim 3. No Lodge under this jurisdiction and within this State, ~hall be represented by a proxy who is not a member of the Lodge.

ARTICLE VIII.
POWERS OF THE GRAND LODGl:.
SECTION 1. 'l'he Grand Lodge has original and exclusive jurisdiction over all
subjects of Masonic legislation, and appellate jurisdiction only from the decisions of the subordinate Lodges ; and its enactments and decisions upon all questions shall be the supreme Masonic law of the State. It shall also prescribe such
rules and regulations for the government of the subordinate Lodges, as will, In
its judgment, conduce to the welfare, prosperity and happiness of the Craft ; and
may grant Dispensations and Charters for the establishment of new Lodges, and
may revoke and annul the same, for such causes as it may deem su11lcient. It
shall prescribe the manner, and shall require a uniform mode of working ; and
may require from the subordinate Lodges such reasonable duea and feu, as will
at all times discharge the engagements of the Grand Lodge.

its regular dues ; and, in case of the non-performance of these duties, its representatives may be debarred from all the privileges of this Grand Lodge, and its

S11:c. 9. It is not competent for a Lodge to expel or suspend a member from
the rights and privileges of Masonry, for the non-payment of dues; but any

six months, except in case of protracted illness, or absence from the State, may

stricken from the roll shall not be received as a member of any other Lodge until he shall have paid up all arrearages to the Lodge of which he was last a member ; and, in the event of the non-existence of said Lodge, to the Grand Lodge.
SEC. 10. All complaints and charges brought against a brother before a Lodge,
proper to be written, shall be reduced to writing, and filed with the Secretary ;
a copy of which shall be served upon the accused, at leaat ten days before he is
arraigned for trial, and after trial bad, should the accused be suspended or expelled from the rights and privileges of Masonry, it shall be the duty of the
Lodge to report the fact to the Grand Lodge at its next stated meeting.
SEc. 11. In all cases of suspension or expulsion by a subordinate Lodge, the
right of appeal lies to the Grand Lodge ; but no such appeal shall be entertained
unless prosecuted at the stated meeting of the Grand Lodge next ensuing the
time of the decision from which the appeal is made · and no suspension or expulsion shall be published until the Grand Lodge sb!h have cognizance thereof.
The Grand Lodge shall prescribe rules and regulations for the trial of appeals.
SEC. 12. No appeal from any decision of the Master of a Lodge shall be
taken to the body of the Lodge ; but five members of any subordinate Lodge
may prefer charges to the Grand Master, or, in his absence, to the Deputy Grand
Master, against the Master of said Lodge, who, upon the he.aring of said charges,
shall, if be deem necessary, suspend such Master from the exercise of the duties
of his office, until the next Annual Gra.nd Communication.
SEC. 13. No Entered Apprentice, or Fellow Craft Mason, shall be advanced
to a superior degree, in any Lodge other than that in which he received the previous degree, unless by the consent, in writing, of that Lodge, if said Lodge be
at the time in existence.
SEC. 14. On the rejection of an applicant for initiation by any Lodge under
the jurisdiction of 'this Grand Lodge, the Secretary of said Lodge shall forthwith
notify all the Lodges in said jurisdiction thereof, and no Lodge shall be allowed
to receive bis petition short of one year from such rejection.
SEC. 15. A book shall be kept by the Secretary of each subordinate Lodge,
alphabetically arranged, in which shall be registered the names of all persons
stricken from the roll, expelled, suspended or rejected, together with the name
of the Lodge, and date of the event so recorded.

REGULATION
OF TIIE

8ranb tobgt of <!talifornia~
RELATIVE TO TRIALS,
JS AMENDED MA.Y, J, L, 5856.

SECTION I.
Whenever a member of a Lodge, or a Brother, under this jurisdiction, shall
be accused of any offence which, if proved, would subject him to suspension or
expulsion, the proceedings in the premises shall be conducted agreeably to the
following rules : RuLE l. The accusation shall be made in writing, under the signature of a
Master Mason, and given in charge of the Secretary of the Lodge, who, under
the direction of the Master, shall serve, or cause the accused to be served, with
an attested copy of the charges, ten days at least, previous to the time appointed
for the examination : Provided, The residence of the accused shall be known,
and shall be within the distance of fifty miles of the place where the Lodge,
having the· matter in hand, is located. If the residence of the accused be at a
greater distance than fifty miles, but within the State, then, and in that case, a
summons to appear and show cause, forwarded to him by mail, or other conveyance, twenty days at least, before the time of trial, shall be considered sufficient service. If bis residence be out of the State, and unknown, the Lodge
may proceed to examine the charges, ex parte; but if known, a summons shall
be sent him by mail, or otherwise, four months, at least, before the time appointed for the examination.
RuLE 2. The examination of the charges shall be had in a Lodge specially
notified and convened. for the purpose, at which no visitors shall be admitted,
except as counsel or witnesses.
RuLE 3. The accused may select any brother for bis counsel, and the witnesses shall testify, if Masons, on their honor, as such. Hearsay evidence shall
be excluded.
RULE 4. The question, "Is the accused guilty or not giiilty ?" shall be distinctly put to each member of the Lodge, by name, commencing with the
youngest. The vote of each member shall be given by ballot, and the Secretary
shall record the result thereof, which shall be the decision of the Lodge.
RuLF: 5. If the verdict be suspension or expulsion, the name of the person so
suspended or expelled shall be sent up at the ensuing meeting of this Grand
Lodge for examination ; and if no appeal be taken, the action shall be final.
Rur..E 6. A sentence of expulsion shall not take effect until confirmed by this
Grand Lodge ; but shall operate as a suspension of the delinquent, in the meantime. In all cases a majority of two thirds shall be necessary to suspend or
expel.
RuLE 7. When a sentence of expulsion or suspension shall be pronounced
by any Lodge, the Secretary of such Lodge, under its seal, shall Immediately
notify all the subordinate Lodges and the Grand Secretary of such event.
SECTION II.
RuLE 1. A suspension or expulsion of a Brother from a Royal Arch Chapter,
or an Encampmen~ of Knights Templar, shall not operate as an expulsion from
the Lodge of which he is a member.
